glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The LORD honors those who honor Him and brings low those who treat Him as unimportant.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Hannah has dedicated Samuel at Shiloh, where he serves under Eli before Israel has a king. Her song opens the chapter, and Samuel’s growth is set beside the corruption of Eli’s sons and the announced judgment on their house.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Therefore the LORD God of Israel says: ‘I said indeed that your house and the house of your father would walk before Me forever.’ But now the LORD says: ‘Far be it from Me; for those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed.” (1 Samuel 2:30, NKJV)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Hannah sings that God overturns whatever people trust in, and the chapter proves her right: Samuel, a child with no standing, grows before the LORD, while Eli’s house, secure in its office, is judged. What separates them is not position but whether God is given His place.

Hannah has just left her son at Shiloh, and she answers with a song rather than a lament. She does not thank God only for a child. She praises Him as the holy Rock who breaks the bow of the mighty, feeds the hungry, opens the barren womb, and lifts the poor from the ash heap. Hannah’s song declares what God is like, and the story that follows shows Him acting in accordance with her praise.

Samuel now serves in a sanctuary whose priests do not know the LORD. Hophni and Phinehas are priests by birth, but they “did not know the LORD.” They seize the best of the sacrifice before the fat is burned, threaten worshipers who object, and use their position at the tabernacle door to satisfy their appetites. The account moves back and forth between Samuel and Eli’s sons, who serve at the same sanctuary. Samuel ministers, wears the little robe his mother brings each year, and grows. Eli’s sons take, ignore their father’s rebuke, and move toward death. Eli himself stands between them, a man who speaks the right words and does not act on them.

Then God speaks directly. A man of God reminds Eli of everything his family was given and charges him with honoring his sons above the LORD. The privilege that should have bound Eli’s house to God becomes the ground of its judgment. Yet the chapter does not end in ruin alone. God promises a faithful priest who will act according to His heart and mind, and the bread the hungry sang about in verse 5 is what Eli’s descendants will beg for in verse 36.

Shiloh, in the hill country of Ephraim, holds the tabernacle in the days of the judges, before Israel has a king. Eli is the senior priest, and his sons serve with him. Samuel’s home is Ramah, and his parents come up each year to sacrifice. Religious life is centered on this one place, which is why the corruption of its priests reaches so far.

Chapter 1 ended with a barren woman’s vow kept. Chapter 3 opens with the word of the LORD “rare in those days,” and chapter 4 carries out what the man of God announced: Hophni and Phinehas die on one day, the ark is captured, and Eli dies at the news. Chapter 2 is the hinge between Hannah’s answered prayer and the collapse of the old order. It also opens a frame around the whole book. Hannah’s song and David’s song near the end (2 Samuel 22) both call the LORD a Rock, and both close with His king and His anointed.

Hannah’s song is itself framed by a horn. “My horn is exalted in the LORD” opens it in verse 1, and God exalting “the horn of His anointed” closes it in verse 10, so that a woman’s private vindication widens into the hope of a king. The narrative moves in a matching rhythm, with Samuel’s growth (vv. 11, 18–21, 26) set between the scenes of Eli’s sons (vv. 12–17, 22–25), and the reader is left to weigh the two lives side by side. Bread supplies the last reversal: those “full” who hire themselves out for bread in verse 5 become Eli’s house begging for a morsel of it in verse 36.

Every figure in this chapter answers the same question: who stands first? Hannah rejoices in the LORD before she rejoices in the son she has given back. Samuel ministers to Him in a linen ephod, a priestly garment, long before anyone knows what he will become. Hophni and Phinehas treat His offering as their own, and Eli, by failing to restrain them, honors his sons above Him. The LORD answers each in kind.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
1 Samuel 2:1–10 — Hannah’s Song of the LORD Who Brings Low and Lifts Up

Hannah praises the holy LORD who weighs actions, brings low the proud and strong, and raises the weak and needy. Her song ends with prophetic anticipation of His king and His anointed, before Israel has a king.

1 Samuel 2:11–17 — The Contempt of Eli’s Sons

Samuel ministers before Eli, while Eli’s sons, who do not know the LORD, seize the people’s sacrifices and threaten worshipers who object. Their contempt for the LORD’s offering makes their sin very great before Him.

1 Samuel 2:18–21 — Samuel Ministers and Hannah Is Blessed

Samuel ministers in a linen ephod, and Hannah brings him a little robe each year. Eli blesses his parents, the LORD gives Hannah three sons and two daughters, and Samuel grows before Him.

1 Samuel 2:22–26 — Eli’s Rebuke Goes Unheeded

Eli confronts his sons about their evil, but they refuse to heed him, and the narrator states that the LORD desired to kill them. Samuel’s growth in favor with God and people stands beside their persistent rebellion.

1 Samuel 2:27–36 — A Man of God Announces Judgment on Eli’s House

A man of God charges Eli with honoring his sons above the LORD and announces judgment on his house, with the death of both sons on one day as the sign. The LORD also promises a faithful priest and a sure house.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Samuel’s rise is not accidental. The book is built on the pattern Hannah sings, where God brings down established strength and raises what looks insignificant. Eli’s house falls and Samuel rises here; Saul falls and David rises later. The song teaches the reader how to read the rest of the book.

Office does not guarantee knowing God. Hophni and Phinehas hold every credential Israel’s worship could give, yet they do not know the LORD. Samuel holds none of them and ministers before Him. The chapter also marks a shift in leadership: authority moves away from a priestly house that has failed and toward a man whom God is forming in quiet. That shift prepares the way for the prophet who will anoint Israel’s first two kings.

God takes seriously how His name, His offering, and His people are treated. The chapter’s judgment is not a burst of anger. It comes after privilege, after warning, and after long tolerance of what Eli knew was wrong.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Reversal

Hannah’s song is a catalog of turnings: the strong are broken, the hungry are filled, the barren bears, the poor sit with princes. The chapter enacts them. The song is not a formula that guarantees every outcome, but it declares that no condition lies outside God’s rule.

Knowing God and Holding Office

Priests who do not know the LORD stand beside a child who ministers to Him. The chapter distinguishes religious position from a real relationship with God. Without that relationship, the priests’ conduct was governed by appetite, custom, and self-interest.

Honor and Contempt

God’s verdict on Eli’s house is spoken in terms of honor. Eli honors his sons more than God, and Hophni and Phinehas treat God’s offering with contempt. The chapter presents this as the root failure, one that Eli’s rebuke fails to reach.

Leaders Who Take

The sons of Eli grab what belongs to God and to the worshipers, and the text sees that as a leadership failure, not merely a private sin. Eli sees it too, and does not restrain them. The pattern of leaders who take rather than serve returns in Samuel’s warning about a king in chapter 8.

Quiet Preparation

While a priesthood collapses, God is growing a boy. Samuel’s advance is described in small steps, year by year, in a place where nobody would have expected a leader to form. The chapter shows that God can begin preparing what comes next even while a failing structure remains in place.

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Horn

A horn stands for strength and dignity, and it frames the song. Hannah’s horn is exalted in verse 1; God exalts the horn of His anointed in verse 10.

Know

In this context, to know the LORD means more than possessing information about Him. The lives of Hophni and Phinehas show no genuine recognition, reverence, or submission, while Samuel “ministered to the LORD.” The chapter sets the two side by side.

Honor and Light

The Hebrew kabed means heavy, weighty; qalal means light. God tells Eli that those who honor Him will be honored and those who despise Him will be lightly esteemed. The play on words governs the oracle and returns in Ichabod’s name (4:21), where “glory” is from the same root as “honor.”

Anointed

The Hebrew word mashiach means “anointed one.” Here it refers to the king God will establish, and the word carries the trajectory of the book toward David and, in the larger story of Scripture, toward the Messiah.

culture.title: HONOR || Through His Eyes
culture.statement: Relationships are protected when we ascribe heaven’s value to the people around us. Like Jesus, we choose to interact with people, not as they deserve, but according to their God given value.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 2
culture.html:
Honor is a central issue in this chapter, and it appears in more than one way.

Giving God His rightful place. The chapter’s own language of honor begins with God. The Hebrew word for honor carries the sense of weight: we give God the weight His worth deserves when other loyalties compete. God told Eli, “you … honor your sons more than Me” (2:29), and declared, “those who honor Me I will honor” (2:30). Honoring God means valuing Him above every competing loyalty and acting accordingly.

Valuing people through heaven’s eyes means not treating people as if they existed for our benefit. Eli’s sons treated worshipers as a source of meat, demanded God’s portion for themselves, and threatened force when challenged (2:13–16). Their sexual misconduct further dishonored those serving at the tabernacle (2:22). These were “the LORD’S people” (2:24), not people who existed for the priests’ benefit. Honor recognizes their God-given value and treats them accordingly for their value to God, not their value to us.

Misplaced honor. Eli rebuked his sons, but he did not restrain them (2:22–25; 3:13). God’s verdict was that he honored his sons above the LORD (2:29). Honoring family cannot mean allowing them to dishonor God or harm His people. Heaven’s value must govern both our relationships and the decisions those relationships require.

Honor through God’s eyes. Hannah’s song shows what heaven’s value looks like. God “raises the poor from the dust and lifts the beggar from the ash heap, to set them among princes” (2:8). The world’s ranking of who matters is not His. The chapter therefore gives us a picture of Honor at East Gate: people are valued according to what God says about them, whether they sit on a refuse heap, hold a priestly office, or are a child in a linen ephod, and God Himself honors those who honor Him.

culture.title: We are People of the Word
culture.statement: The Holy Bible is the only infallible and final authority for Christian faith and life. The Holy Scriptures are timeless, inerrant and are to be read personally, discerned corporately, and walked out in community. We interpret all Scripture through the life and teachings of Jesus, trusting Holy Spirit to reveal truth and transform us as we submit ourselves fully to God’s revealed Word.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 2
culture.html:
The chapter shows what happens when custom replaces commandment, and what happens when a person stays anchored in what God has said.

Custom against commandment. The priests’ “custom” (mishpat) with the people was to send a servant with a three-pronged fork to take whatever came up (2:13–14). God’s law had already said which portions belonged to the priests, and that the fat belonged to the LORD and must be burned first (Leviticus 3:16; 7:28–34). Eli’s sons replaced God’s instructions with a procedure that served themselves. “The way we have always done it” does not make something right. The standard remains what God has said.

A worshiper who held to the Word. When the servant demanded meat, an ordinary Israelite answered, “They should really burn the fat first” (2:16). He knew what God required and appealed to it when the priest’s servant demanded otherwise. As people of the Word, we all need to know Scripture so we can recognize when instruction or practice conflicts with what God has said and avoid being misled.

God’s word comes to pass. The man of God speaks, “Thus says the LORD” (2:27), and announces that Eli’s sons will die on the same day (2:34). Chapter 4 records the fulfillment. As people of the Word, we need to remember that God’s warnings are as sure as His promises.

culture.title: We are a Tabernacle of David
culture.statement: We were created to delight the Father and host His presence. As we embrace His ways, our lives become continual offerings of praise—both personally and together. We live with unhindered access to God, ministering to Him first and carrying His presence wherever we go. As His dwelling is restored among us, we become a people through whom the nations are drawn to seek the Lord.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 2
culture.html:
Samuel’s service and Hannah’s praise show lives offered to the LORD.

Ministering to Him first. Samuel “ministered to the LORD” (2:11) and “ministered before the LORD” (2:18). His service was directed toward God. Eli’s sons, although serving at the sanctuary, “did not know the LORD” (2:12) and used their position to satisfy themselves. As a people called to host His presence, we minister to Him first above all else.

Lives as offerings of praise. Hannah’s song is a picture of worship offered from a whole life. Having entrusted Samuel and given Samuel back to the LORD, she rejoices, “My heart rejoices in the LORD” (2:1). Her praise and her surrender belong together. Our lives become continual offerings of praise as our actions, as well as our songs, express our devotion and worship to Him.

focus: Chapter 2 sets Hannah’s prophetic song beside the corruption of Eli’s sons, contrasting the God who brings low and lifts up with priests who despise His offering. While the boy Samuel grows before the LORD, a man of God announces judgment on Eli’s house.

sections.title: Hannah’s Song of the LORD Who Brings Low and Lifts Up
sections.summary: Hannah rejoices in the LORD’s salvation, His incomparable holiness, and His sovereign reversals, in which the proud are humbled and the poor are raised from the dust. She ends by declaring that He will give strength to His king and “exalt the horn of His anointed.”

items.title: One Answered Prayer Taught Hannah How God Runs the World (1 Samuel 2:1–10)
items.html: The song begins with “my heart,” “my horn,” “my mouth” (v. 1) and ends with “the ends of the earth,” “His king,” and “His anointed” (v. 10). Hannah starts with her personal deliverance (v. 1), turns to the character of God (vv. 2–3), widens to His dealings with all humanity, the proud and the poor, the living and the dead (vv. 4–8), and crescendos in prophetic revelation about the ends of the earth and the coming Messiah (vv. 9–10). Very quickly the song loses sight of Samuel altogether. She discerned in her own experience the general laws of God’s dealings with the world. Her prayer in 1:11 asked for one son; her praise in 2:1–10 sees a kingdom. This is the anatomy of mature worship: it uses the personal miracle as a launchpad to declare the universal majesty and eternal purposes of God. When a believer’s personal agony is resolved in God’s presence, the praise that follows breaks the boundaries of that individual life; true gratitude catapults the soul into prophetic alignment. God’s private kindness to one person is a window on how He governs history and where He is taking it. When God answers us, He is not only meeting a need; He is showing us Himself.
items.q: The song begins with “my heart,”

items.title: The Principle of the Great Reversal (1 Samuel 2:1–11)
items.html: The dominant theme of these verses is the great reversal. Bows are broken, stumblers are strengthened, the full go hungry, the barren bears seven, the poor are seated with princes. God consistently opposes the proud and exalts the humble. His kingdom runs on an inverted economy: He bypasses the proud, the resourced, and the powerful to accomplish His purposes through the broken, the empty, and the desperate. This section is the theological overture to the books of Samuel, and indeed to the whole Bible, and it introduces for the first time the “anointed” King, tying God’s final victory over darkness to a coming Messiah. The pattern plays out at once: God bypasses Eli’s powerful house for a little boy named Samuel, and later bypasses tall King Saul for a shepherd boy named David. Eli’s house falls, Samuel rises; Saul falls, David rises. History is not driven by strength, status, or institutions, but by the God who “brings low and lifts up.” We should expect His great reversals.
items.q: The dominant theme of these verses is the great reversal.

items.title: First the Sacrifice, Then the Song (1 Samuel 1:28; 2:1, 11)
items.html: Hannah sang on the day she gave her son away (1:28; 2:11), not on the day she received him. First the sacrifice, then the song. So it was when Hezekiah restored temple worship: “when the burnt offering began, the song of the LORD also began” (2 Chronicles 29:27). Mary’s song came after her surrender: “Let it be to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). The deepest worship in this chapter comes not from receiving but from releasing. Families who dedicate a child, ministries that hand off something precious, believers who place a dream back in God’s hands, often find that the song comes on the far side of the sacrifice, not before it.
items.q: Hannah sang on the day she gave her son away (1:28; 2:11), not on the day she received him.

items.title: A Mother’s Song and a King’s Song Frame the Books of Samuel (1 Samuel 2:1–10; 2 Samuel 22:1–51)
items.html: The books of Samuel open with Hannah’s song and close, before the appendices, with David’s song, and the two share their vocabulary: horn (2:1, 10; 2 Samuel 22:3), rock (2:2; 2 Samuel 22:2–3, 32), salvation (2:1; 2 Samuel 22:3), the grave (2:6; 2 Samuel 22:6), thunder from heaven (2:10; 2 Samuel 22:14), king and anointed (2:10; 2 Samuel 22:51). Both celebrate the LORD as Rock and speak of His anointed king. David’s last line, “He is the tower of salvation to His king, and shows mercy to His anointed” (2 Samuel 22:51), answers Hannah’s last line. What God begins in a woman’s prayer He completes in a king’s praise, and everything in between, Samuel’s call, Saul’s fall, David’s rise, is the outworking of one song. It has rightly been called a golden key to the whole book.
items.q: The books of Samuel open with Hannah’s song and close, before the appendices, with David’s song, and the two share their vocabulary: horn (2:1, 10; 2 Samuel 22:3), rock (2:2; 2 Samuel 22:2–3, 32), salvation (2:1; 2 Samuel 22:3), the grave (2:6; 2 Samuel 22:6), thunder from heaven (2:10; 2 Samuel 22:14), king and anointed (2:10; 2 Samuel 22:51).

items.title: Two Mothers’ Songs and One Horn of Salvation (1 Samuel 2:1–10; Luke 1:46–55, 68–69)
items.html: Mary’s Magnificat follows Hannah’s song throughout: “He has put down the mighty from their thrones, and exalted the lowly. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich He has sent away empty” (Luke 1:52–53; compare 2:4–8). Both mothers celebrate a God who scatters the proud and lifts the humble, and both sing because of a miraculously given son. Zacharias takes Hannah’s last line and names it: God “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David” (Luke 1:69). Hannah rejoiced in “Your salvation,” yeshu’ah (v. 1), and the child Mary carried was named Yeshua. Hannah’s song describes the reversal; Mary’s song names the Person who brings it. Hannah’s horn is exalted in Samuel; the world’s horn of salvation is raised in Jesus. The lowly mother lifted by God in Shiloh points to the lowly Son lifted by God from the grave (v. 6; Philippians 2:8–9), and everything Hannah praised finds its center in Him.
items.q: Mary’s Magnificat follows Hannah’s song throughout: “He has put down the mighty from their thrones, and exalted the lowly.

sections.title: The Contempt of Eli’s Sons
sections.summary: Elkanah returns home while the child ministers to the LORD before Eli. Eli’s sons, who did not know the LORD, take the people’s sacrifices by force, and their sin is very great before the LORD.

sections.title: Samuel Ministers and Hannah Is Blessed
sections.summary: Samuel ministers before the LORD in a linen ephod, and Hannah brings him a little robe each year. Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah, the LORD gives her three sons and two daughters, and Samuel grows before the LORD.

sections.title: Eli’s Rebuke Goes Unheeded
sections.summary: The aged Eli hears of all his sons’ evil and rebukes them, but they do not heed their father, because the LORD desired to kill them. In contrast, the child Samuel grows in stature and in favor with the LORD and with men.

items.title: The Narrator’s Alternating Camera (1 Samuel 2:11–26)
items.html: The section cuts back and forth like a cinematic montage: the sons’ greed (vv. 12–17); “But Samuel” (v. 18); Hannah’s robe and Eli’s blessing (vv. 19–21); the sons’ immorality and Eli’s weak rebuke (vv. 22–25); “And the child Samuel grew” (v. 26). The two families are woven together so that each sets off the other. The sons grew on in sin while the child grew on in favor; God loves to watch His lilies grow among thorns. On one side the established religious machinery is rotting from the inside, marked by greed, sexual immorality, and cynical profiteering from the things of God; on the other a quiet, obscure boy in a linen ephod is growing in favor with God and people. Light and darkness grow up side by side in the same house, and God is watching both. This juxtaposition shows that spiritual environment does not dictate spiritual destiny. Hophni and Phinehas had every advantage and became corrupt; Samuel was placed in a toxic, backslidden environment and grew in holiness. That is a word of hope for parents, and for believers in compromised churches and cultures: the atmosphere does not have to decide the outcome. Whenever there are men like Eli’s sons, God raises up someone like Samuel. God is never left without a witness. He does not wait for corruption to end before He raises its replacement; He grows the answer in the same courtyard, often in a child no one is watching.
items.q: The section cuts back and forth like a cinematic montage: the sons’ greed (vv. 12–17); “But Samuel” (v. 18); Hannah’s robe and Eli’s blessing (vv. 19–21); the sons’ immorality and Eli’s weak rebuke (vv. 22–25); “And the child Samuel grew” (v. 26).

items.title: The Rotting Institution and the Hidden Seed (1 Samuel 2:12–26)
items.html: God does not always tear down a corrupt religious structure with a lightning bolt. Often His judgment on a rotting institution is simply to let it die under the weight of its own compromise, while He quietly, almost unnoticed, grows a pure alternative seed right in its shadow. Extortion at the altar and immorality at the door are followed again and again by the quiet refrain: “But Samuel ministered before the LORD.” God’s answer to deep systemic corruption is a devoted child wearing a linen ephod.
items.q: God does not always tear down a corrupt religious structure with a lightning bolt.

items.title: Two Kinds of Young Men at Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:11, 13, 15, 17, 18, 21, 26)
items.html: The same Hebrew word, na’ar, “boy, young man, servant,” describes the priest’s servant with the fork (vv. 13, 15), the “young men” whose sin was very great (v. 17), and Samuel, “the child” who ministered (vv. 11, 18, 21, 26). Same age group, same courtyard, same sanctuary, opposite service. One young servant came to take from worshipers; the other came to serve the LORD. Young people around ministry are always being formed by what they see. Leaders should ask which kind of na’ar their example is producing, and young believers should know that their surroundings do not decide which one they become.
items.q: The same Hebrew word, na’ar, “boy, young man, servant,” describes the priest’s servant with the fork (vv. 13, 15), the “young men” whose sin was very great (v. 17), and Samuel, “the child” who ministered (vv. 11, 18, 21, 26).

items.title: Eli Raised Another Woman’s Son to Faithfulness and Lost His Own (1 Samuel 2:11–26; 3:9–10)
items.html: Eli supervised Samuel’s service (v. 11), blessed his parents (v. 20), and later taught him how to answer God’s call (3:9). He could not have been a wholly bad father, since he helped raise Samuel to godliness. Yet his own sons “did not know the LORD” (v. 12). Eli’s failure was not an inability to teach; it was an unwillingness to confront those closest to him (v. 29). Grace does not run in the blood: God gave it to the child of an obscure country Levite and not to the sons of the high priest. Leaders can be effective with other people’s children and blind at home. The test of a spiritual father is not only whom he mentors but whom he is willing to correct.
items.q: Eli supervised Samuel’s service (v. 11), blessed his parents (v. 20), and later taught him how to answer God’s call (3:9).

items.title: Correction That Came Too Late and Too Soft (1 Samuel 1:14; 2:22–25; 3:13)
items.html: Eli was quick and severe with Hannah, accusing a praying woman of drunkenness (1:14), and slow and mild with his own sons. He seems to have spoken only after the immorality became public (v. 22), not when the greed began (vv. 13–17); had he rebuked them for their greed, the rest might have been prevented. His words were a question (v. 23), an appeal to reputation (v. 24), and a theological observation (v. 25), with no action. God later names the root: “his sons made themselves vile, and he did not restrain them” (3:13). The Lord’s rebuke of Eli was as hard as Eli’s rebuke of his sons had been soft. Parents and pastors who correct early, clearly, and with action are not being unkind; they are being merciful before mercy runs out.
items.q: Eli was quick and severe with Hannah, accusing a praying woman of drunkenness (1:14), and slow and mild with his own sons.

items.title: The Table Where God Shared a Meal With His People (1 Samuel 2:13–17; Leviticus 7:11–21; Deuteronomy 12:7)
items.html: The peace offering was the one sacrifice that became a meal. The fat went up to God, the priest received his assigned share, and the worshiper’s family ate the rest “before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice” (Deuteronomy 12:7). The worshiper’s portion was a token of communion and fellowship with God. Hophni and Phinehas plunged their fork into that fellowship meal and seized God’s portion before Him. The result was that “men abhorred the offering of the LORD” (v. 17): people lost the joy of eating in God’s presence. God has always wanted to dwell and dine with His people; Jesus still says, “I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with Me” (Revelation 3:20). The gravest damage of corrupt ministry is not only stolen meat but a spoiled table, where people stop expecting to meet God.
items.q: The peace offering was the one sacrifice that became a meal.

items.title: Appetite Tells You Who Your God Is (1 Samuel 2:12–17, 22)
items.html: The priests wanted meat, then the fat, then women (v. 22), a steady escalation of appetite. Paul describes such people as those “whose god is their belly” (Philippians 3:19). Sin is preferring lesser pleasures to God, and Hophni and Phinehas are a portrait of desire gone wrong: they would rather have a roast than the Lord. The cure for disordered appetite is not mere restraint but a greater delight.
items.q: The priests wanted meat, then the fat, then women (v. 22), a steady escalation of appetite.

items.title: The Anatomy of a Dying Ministry (1 Samuel 2:12–25)
items.html: This section exposes the warning signs of a spiritual house about to collapse. First, the loss of the knowledge of God (v. 12). Second, personal appetite raised above God’s requirements (v. 15). Third, manipulation and force used to get one’s way (v. 16). Fourth, toleration of gross immorality (v. 22). Finally, the rationalization and passive management of sin by the senior leader (v. 23). When these line up, the lampstand of that ministry is about to be removed (Revelation 2:5).
items.q: This section exposes the warning signs of a spiritual house about to collapse.

items.title: “Who Will Intercede?” Is Answered in the Next Verse (1 Samuel 2:25–26; 7:5–9; 12:23)
items.html: Eli asks, “If a man sins against the LORD, who will intercede for him?” (v. 25). The very next sentence is, “And the child Samuel grew” (v. 26). Samuel becomes Israel’s great intercessor. At Mizpah he “cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him” (7:9). At Saul’s coronation he says, “far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you” (12:23), using the same “far be it” God spoke against Eli’s house (2:30). Psalm 99:6 lists Samuel “among those who called upon His name,” and God names Moses and Samuel as Israel’s great intercessors (Jeremiah 15:1). Eli’s question had an answer growing in his own courtyard, and that answer points beyond itself to the One who “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25). God answers the hopeless questions of one generation with the people He is raising in the next.
items.q: Eli asks, “If a man sins against the LORD, who will intercede for him?” (v. 25).

items.title: Leaders Who Take and a Mother Who Gives (1 Samuel 2:13–16, 19–20; 8:9–17; 12:3–4)
items.html: This section is full of taking: the priest “would take for himself” (v. 14); “you may take,” “I will take it by force” (v. 16). Against that stands Hannah, who brings a robe “year by year” (v. 19) and has given her son as “the loan … given to the LORD” (v. 20). The thread runs through the book. The priests’ “custom” (mishpat, v. 13) is echoed by “the behavior (mishpat) of the king,” which Samuel describes with a string of “he will take” (8:9–17). The corruption of leadership in Israel starts at the altar before it reaches the throne. And at the end of his ministry Samuel asks Israel, “Whose ox have I taken?” and they answer, “You have not … taken anything from any man’s hand” (12:3–4). The book measures every leader by whether he takes or gives. The question for every leader in God’s house is the same: are people poorer or richer for my ministry?
items.q: The question for every leader in God’s house is the same: are people poorer or richer for my ministry?

items.title: The Robe and the Fork (1 Samuel 2:13–14, 19)
items.html: Two objects capture this section: the priests’ three-pronged fork, stabbing into worshipers’ offerings to take what was not theirs, and Hannah’s little robe, carried each year to clothe what she had given away. One pictures religion that takes; the other pictures love that gives. The contrast is a quiet sermon on the difference between consuming ministry and self-giving devotion.
items.q: Two objects capture this section: the priests’ three-pronged fork, stabbing into worshipers’ offerings to take what was not theirs, and Hannah’s little robe, carried each year to clothe what she had given away.

sections.title: A Man of God Announces Judgment on Eli’s House
sections.summary: A man of God charges Eli with honoring his sons above the LORD and announces that his house will lose its privileged place, with the death of Hophni and Phinehas on one day as the sign. The LORD will raise up for Himself a faithful priest and build him a sure house.

groups.title: A Prophecy Against the House of Eli

items.title: The Transition of Covenants (1 Samuel 2:27–36)
items.html: This passage marks a monumental shift in redemptive history. God had promised that the house of Aaron, and Eli’s branch of it, would walk before Him forever (v. 30). Yet here God says, “Far be it from Me.” The Levitical priesthood required covenant faithfulness, and God would not allow His holiness to be endlessly mocked; He removed the lampstand from Eli’s line because it honored men above God. But God’s ultimate purpose cannot be thwarted by human failure. In the middle of devastating judgment He plants a seed of messianic hope: “I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest.” Israel’s access to God would not finally depend on the flawed sons of Aaron, but on a priest God Himself provides, who acts entirely according to His heart. The judgment on Eli’s house creates the vacuum that calls for the faithful Priest (v. 35). The failure of the Old Covenant mediators becomes the very stage for the New Covenant Mediator.
items.q: This passage marks a monumental shift in redemptive history.

items.title: The Idolatry of Permissive Love (1 Samuel 2:27–36)
items.html: The man of God strikes at the root of Eli’s failure: “Why do you … honor your sons more than Me?” Eli was not an actively malicious man; he was a passive one. He rebuked his sons with words, but he did not remove them from office. He allowed the desecration of God’s glory in order to preserve his family’s comfort. This section reveals that passivity in leadership, especially tolerating sin out of misplaced family loyalty or fear of conflict, is not viewed by God as mere weakness. It is indicted as high treason and idolatry. Raising human relationships above the holiness of God brings the collapse of spiritual authority.
items.q: The man of God strikes at the root of Eli’s failure: “Why do you … honor your sons more than Me?”

items.title: The Tragedy of Misplaced Loyalty (1 Samuel 2:29–36)
items.html: The whole indictment pivots on one devastating accusation: Eli honored his sons more than God. In trying to save his sons from discipline, he lost his sons entirely; they would die in one day. In trying to preserve his family’s comfort at God’s expense, he condemned his family to poverty and early death (vv. 33, 36). The spiritual paradox is clear: when we put family before God, we end up destroying the family. When we put God before family, we place our family under the covering of His grace, as Hannah did.
items.q: The whole indictment pivots on one devastating accusation: Eli honored his sons more than God.

items.title: The Faithful Priest Who Walks Before the Anointed, and Is the Anointed (1 Samuel 2:10, 35; Zechariah 6:13; Hebrews 2:17; 3:1–6; 7:23–28)
items.html: The chapter ends with two figures: “a faithful priest” and “My anointed” (v. 35), echoing “His king … His anointed” (v. 10). In Israel’s history they were separate. Samuel walked before Saul and David; Zadok walked before Solomon and anointed him with “a horn of oil from the tabernacle” (1 Kings 1:39). Some object that the faithful priest cannot be Christ, because he walks before the anointed. But the prophets foresaw the two offices joined: “He shall be a priest on His throne” (Zechariah 6:13), “a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). Only Jesus perfectly does all that is in the Father’s heart (John 8:29). He is “a merciful and faithful High Priest” (Hebrews 2:17), “faithful … as a Son over His own house, whose house we are” (Hebrews 3:6), who “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25). The faithful Priest and the Anointed King of 1 Samuel 2 meet in one Person, and He is building the sure house that Eli’s line could not keep.
items.q: The chapter ends with two figures: “a faithful priest” and “My anointed” (v. 35), echoing “His king … His anointed” (v. 10).

items.title: Inherited Office Is Not a Permanent Pass (1 Samuel 2:28, 30, 35; 13:13–14; 15:28)
items.html: The house of Aaron had been chosen, given an ephod, and promised to “walk before Me forever” (vv. 28, 30), yet God said, “Far be it from Me.” The same pattern follows Saul: “now your kingdom shall not continue. The LORD has sought for Himself a man after His own heart” (13:14), and “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today” (15:28). Priest and king are both measured by God’s heart (2:35; 13:14), not by title or lineage, and in 1 Samuel God forms and removes leaders by that standard. Office is nothing without character. The heaviest scrutiny falls on those with the greatest privilege, and priestly office, spiritual heritage, and years in ministry are no shelter. Every believer in leadership holds a calling that is a stewardship, not a possession.
items.q: The house of Aaron had been chosen, given an ephod, and promised to “walk before Me forever” (vv. 28, 30), yet God said, “Far be it from Me.”

items.title: God’s House Never Falls for Want of Hands (1 Samuel 2:32, 35; Psalm 78:60, 68–70; Jeremiah 7:12)
items.html: The judgment on Eli’s house is severe, and Shiloh itself would be abandoned: “He forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had placed among men” (Psalm 78:60). Yet the same psalm goes on: God “chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion which He loved,” and “He also chose David His servant” (Psalm 78:68–70). God’s work never falls to the ground for want of hands to carry it on. The chapter that announces the fall of a priestly house also announces a faithful priest and a sure house (v. 35). God’s purposes are never hostage to failing institutions; even as Shiloh decays, He is raising a boy in a linen ephod. When His house is corrupted, He is already preparing what comes next. His purpose to dwell with His people survives the failure of those who served His dwelling. It moved from Shiloh to Zion, from tabernacle to temple, and finally to Christ and His people, “whose house we are” (Hebrews 3:6).
items.q: The judgment on Eli’s house is severe, and Shiloh itself would be abandoned: “He forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had placed among men” (Psalm 78:60).

1.brief: Hannah prays in a song of rejoicing, declaring that her heart rejoices in the LORD and that her horn, a picture of strength and dignity, is exalted in Him. She can smile at her enemies because her joy rests in the LORD’s salvation, not merely in her changed circumstances.
1.explain:
“And Hannah prayed and said:”

Hannah's song follows directly on the dedication of Samuel (1:28). The narrator calls it a prayer, though it is filled with praise. The woman who once prayed silently in bitterness (1:10–13) now prays aloud in joy. The setting is still Shiloh, and the son she has just given to the LORD is with her.

“My heart rejoices in the LORD;”

Her first words center on the LORD. “My heart,” the seat of her inner life that had been grieved (1:8), now “rejoices.” Her joy is “in the LORD,” not first in the child. That order matters. She has just handed Samuel over; her joy rests in the God who answered her.

“My horn is exalted in the LORD.”

“Horn” is a picture of strength and dignity, drawn from the horns of a strong animal such as the wild ox (Deuteronomy 33:17). To have one's horn “exalted” meant to be raised from humiliation to honor and strength (Psalm 75:10). For years Hannah's head had been bowed under Peninnah's taunts; now God had lifted it. The image will return in the last line of the song, where the LORD exalts “the horn of His anointed” (2:10).

“I smile at my enemies,”

“I smile” is literally ‘my mouth is wide over,’ a picture of open-mouthed triumph. Hannah's “enemies” include Peninnah, who provoked her (1:6), but the plural widens the scope. She can face every adversary without fear.

“Because I rejoice in Your salvation.”

The reason is God's “salvation,” His deliverance. Hannah speaks directly to God now (“Your salvation”). Her joy rests in the LORD's saving act, not merely in her changed circumstances. What God had done for one barren woman she understood as salvation, the same word Israel used for the deliverance at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:2).
1.notes:
Hannah's song is Hebrew poetry, built on parallel lines that restate or develop one another.

The Hebrew word for “horn” here and in 2:10 is used as a figure of strength, like the horn of a powerful animal. The same Hebrew word names the literal horn of oil used to anoint David (16:1, 13).

reflections.title: She Praised the Giver, Not the Gift
reflections.html: “My heart rejoices in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD.” Hannah sang this on the day she left her only son at Shiloh (1:28), yet the song never mentions Samuel. She does not say, “My heart rejoices in Samuel”; she overlooks the gift and praises the Giver. The verb for “rejoices” appears only eight times in the Old Testament, usually for the exultant joy of those God has made triumphant (Psalm 5:11; 9:2; 68:3). When God grants a long-awaited breakthrough, mature joy passes through the gift and rests in the Giver. To rejoice in the blessing alone is to quietly idolize it; to rejoice in the Lord is to keep the blessing in its proper place. Joy that rests in a gift leaves when the gift is given away. Joy that rests in the Lord can sing on the walk home. If one of His gifts were placed back in His hands, would we still be able to sing?
reflections.q: If one of His gifts were placed back in His hands, would we still be able to sing?

reflections.title: The Horn of Power Rooted in Surrender
reflections.html: “My horn is exalted.” The horn pictures a wild ox lifting its head in strength; to have one’s horn raised is to be publicly vindicated, strength restored and honor visible (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 92:10). Hannah’s dignity, trampled for years by Peninnah, was restored entirely by God. Grace is the great vindicator of the oppressed. And notice when her horn was lifted: not while she was striving with her rival, not while she was grasping for a child, but after she had surrendered her long-awaited son back to God. Here is a kingdom paradox: spiritual authority and unassailable strength are not secured by getting what we want, but by offering our most treasured desires back to heaven.
reflections.q: “My horn is exalted.”

reflections.title: Let God Lift Your Horn
reflections.html: “My mouth is enlarged over my enemies, because I rejoice in Your salvation.” Literally, her mouth is opened wide, a gesture of vindication. Yet Hannah names no rival and settles no score; she never mentions Peninnah. Her answer to her antagonist is not petty retaliation but a magnificent declaration of God’s saving power. Real victory over human opposition is not found in defending ourselves but in magnifying God so loudly that the enemy’s taunts are drowned out by worship. The believer who waits for God’s vindication is freed from the exhausting work of defending himself. Where are we still trying to lift our own horn, defending our reputation or settling scores, instead of trusting God to vindicate us in His time?
reflections.q: Where are we still trying to lift our own horn, defending our reputation or settling scores, instead of trusting God to vindicate us in His time?

reflections.title: Rejoice in a Salvation That Makes Room
reflections.html: “I rejoice in Your salvation.” The word is yeshu’ah, from a root whose core idea is to be wide or spacious, to bring someone out of a tight place into room. Barrenness had been Hannah’s narrow place; God’s deliverance gave her breathing space. The same root forms the names Joshua and Yeshua, Jesus. Every rescue God gives His people is a small picture of the great, spacious salvation He would one day give in His Son. And Christ Himself is our exalted horn: when we are weak, union with Him gives an unbreakable authority against the enemy.
reflections.q: “I rejoice in Your salvation.”

reflections.title: Back to the Spot Where She Wept
reflections.html: “And Hannah prayed.” It is the same verb used of her prayer in 1:10, but everything else has changed. Then her voice was not heard and only her lips moved (1:13); now she speaks aloud for anyone to hear. Then she prayed in bitterness of soul; now her mouth is opened wide. The woman who poured out her soul in bitterness now pours out praise in the same sanctuary. “Some day you will come to the spot where you wept and prayed,” wrote one old devotional writer, bringing praise instead. God often brings His people back to the place of their tears so that the same place can hear a new song. Is there such a place God may be bringing us back to?
reflections.q: Is there such a place God may be bringing us back to?

reflections.title: Prayer and Praise, One Language
reflections.html: Hannah “prayed,” yet what follows is a song. In the Spirit, deep intercession and high praise are the same language spoken from one heart. The same God who heard her sighs now receives her songs.
reflections.q: Hannah “prayed,” yet what follows is a song.

2.brief: Hannah confesses that no one is holy like the LORD, that there is no God besides Him, and that there is no rock like our God. Her praise moves from what God has done for her to who He is.
2.explain:
“No one is holy like the LORD,”

Hannah's praise moves from what God has done for her to who He is. “Holy” means set apart, utterly distinct, morally pure, and majestic. “No one is holy like the LORD” echoes Moses' song after the Red Sea: “Who is like You, glorious in holiness” (Exodus 15:11). God's holiness is the first quality Hannah names. It will become a theme of the following chapters, when the men of Beth Shemesh cry, “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” (6:20).

“For there is none besides You,”

“There is none besides You” declares that the LORD alone is God. No other god compares with Him because no other god truly exists (compare Deuteronomy 32:39; Isaiah 45:5). Hannah speaks this in the sanctuary at Shiloh, where Eli's sons treated the LORD with contempt.

“Nor is there any rock like our God.”

“Rock” is a common biblical image for God's strength, stability, and protection. Moses sang, “He is the Rock, His work is perfect” (Deuteronomy 32:4). A rock does not move or fail; those who take refuge in it are safe. Hannah calls Him “our God,” widening her praise from her own experience to the whole people.
2.notes: David's song uses the same pairing of God and rock: “For who is God, except the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God?” (Psalm 18:31; compare 2 Samuel 22:32).

reflections.title: No Rock Like Ours
reflections.html: “No one is holy like the LORD, for there is none besides You, nor is there any rock like our God.” “Rock” (tsur) is first used as a name for God in the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 18, 30–31), where it speaks of His changeless faithfulness, and Israelites carried it in their names. Hannah had leaned on a loving husband’s double portion and his “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” (1:5, 8). Now, holding the son she had begged for, she does not call Samuel her rock either. Even God’s best gifts cannot carry the weight of our lives. Build your emotional and spiritual stability on the unchangeable character of God, not on shifting circumstances. Paul says of the rock that followed Israel, “that Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4), the Rock struck for us in the wilderness, and He is the only ground that does not move. What are we leaning on as a rock that is really a gift and not the Giver?
reflections.q: What are we leaning on as a rock that is really a gift and not the Giver?

reflections.title: Holiness That Makes Him a Foundation
reflections.html: Hannah joins two attributes: His holiness, utterly separate and unlike any created thing, and His solidity, a Rock. Holiness is not one attribute among many; it is the overarching reality of His being, entirely “other.” And here is the profound truth: God’s utter separateness from us is precisely what makes Him a dependable foundation for us. Because He is not like anything else, He does not shift like anything else.
reflections.q: Hannah joins two attributes: His holiness, utterly separate and unlike any created thing, and His solidity, a Rock.

reflections.title: Praise Who God Is Before What God Gave
reflections.html: Hannah’s first confession is not “He gave me a son” but “There is none holy like the LORD.” God’s best gift is God Himself. Worship that only celebrates benefits quietly makes God a means rather than the end. Hannah had a child in her arms, yet her song is filled with God.
reflections.q: Hannah’s first confession is not “He gave me a son” but “There is none holy like the LORD.”

reflections.title: A Rock That Is Also a Spring
reflections.html: An old rabbinic reading took “rock” applied to God as “source” or “spring,” a rock that is also a fountain, like the rock that gave water in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6). The Rock that holds us up is the Rock that pours life out.
reflections.q: An old rabbinic reading took “rock” applied to God as “source” or “spring,” a rock that is also a fountain, like the rock that gave water in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6).

3.brief: Hannah warns the proud to stop their arrogant talk, because the LORD is the God of knowledge and He weighs every action. Boasting is foolish before a God who sees and evaluates all that people do.
3.explain:
“Talk no more so very proudly;”

Hannah now addresses the proud directly. “Talk no more so very proudly” warns those who speak arrogantly. The Hebrew repeats the word for ‘proud’ for emphasis, ‘proudly, proudly.’ Peninnah's taunts may be in view, but the warning reaches anyone who boasts against God or His people.

“Let no arrogance come from your mouth,”

“Arrogance” describes insolent, presumptuous speech. The proud speak as though they answer to no one.

“For the LORD is the God of knowledge;”

The reason boasting is foolish is that “the LORD is the God of knowledge.” He knows everything: every word, every motive, every hidden act. Nothing escapes Him.

“And by Him actions are weighed.”

God “weighs” actions, measuring them as on a scale. Proverbs says, “the LORD weighs the spirits” (Proverbs 16:2). He evaluates not only what people do but why they do it. Boasting is foolish before a God who sees and evaluates all that people do. The warning applies within Shiloh itself, where Eli's sons acted as though no one were watching.
3.notes:
The written Hebrew text has lo', ‘not’ (‘and actions are not weighed’), while the traditional reading marked for pronunciation has lo, ‘by Him’ (‘and by Him actions are weighed’), which the NKJV follows. The two words sound alike in Hebrew.

The traditional reading fits the context and is followed by most translations.

reflections.title: The Proud Count; God Weighs
reflections.html: “For the LORD is the God of knowledge, and by Him actions are weighed.” “God of knowledge” is plural in Hebrew, “God of all knowings,” an intensive form for complete, exhaustive knowledge. “Weighed” means to measure against a standard, the word Proverbs uses when “the LORD weighs the hearts” (Proverbs 16:2; 21:2; 24:12). In Elkanah’s house everything had been counted: Peninnah’s children, the portions on the plate, the years of barrenness (1:4–7). God does not count; He weighs. He does not measure what we bring; He weighs it. Two actions can look identical on the outside and carry completely different spiritual weight. Human beings weigh the outcome of actions; God weighs the motives behind them. Loud words can be very light, and quiet faithfulness can be very heavy, on the scales that matter. Where do we count what is visible while God is weighing what is hidden?
reflections.q: Where do we count what is visible while God is weighing what is hidden?

reflections.title: Busy and Weightless
reflections.html: A massive volume of religious activity can weigh nothing at all on the scales of heaven if it lacks the substance of love and reverence. Eli’s sons were performing the outward mechanics of the priesthood, yet their actions had no spiritual mass; they are called “worthless,” men of Belial, “without profit,” without weight (v. 12). True spiritual substance is determined by the hidden motive, the reverence, and the alignment with God’s heart that fill the action.
reflections.q: A massive volume of religious activity can weigh nothing at all on the scales of heaven if it lacks the substance of love and reverence.

reflections.title: “Talk No More”
reflections.html: “Talk no more so very proudly; let no arrogance come from your mouth.” Hannah had lived for years under a rival’s tongue (1:6–7). Now that God has answered, she does not answer Peninnah by name, mock her, or recount her cruelty. She simply tells pride to stop talking, because the God of knowledge has already heard everything. Peninnah’s taunts are silenced not by Hannah’s retaliation but by the scales of divine justice. Vindication from God does not need to be followed by revenge from us; God’s scales are perfectly calibrated. When God has spoken for us, we can stop speaking against others. Is there proud or careless speech in our lives that we would be ashamed to have placed on those scales?
reflections.q: Is there proud or careless speech in our lives that we would be ashamed to have placed on those scales?

reflections.title: Pride Is a Failure to Know Who Knows
reflections.html: Hannah ties human arrogance directly to human ignorance. Pride is at root a failure to realize that God sees and knows everything. When the reality of His knowledge dawns on a soul, the mouth naturally shuts. Every proud word, Peninnah’s or ours, is placed on God’s scales, and none escapes the final audit.
reflections.q: Hannah ties human arrogance directly to human ignorance.

reflections.title: Old Sayings Silenced
reflections.html: The word for “arrogance” may mean hard or worn-out sayings, perhaps the stock insults heaped on barren women. Through the books of Samuel, God humbles the proud one after another: Peninnah, Eli’s sons, the Philistines, Goliath, Saul, Nabal, Absalom. Hannah’s line is the first notice of a pattern the whole story will keep.
reflections.q: The word for “arrogance” may mean hard or worn-out sayings, perhaps the stock insults heaped on barren women.

4.brief: The bows of mighty warriors are broken, while those who stumbled are clothed with strength. The first of the song’s reversals shows that human strength does not decide who stands.
4.explain:
“The bows of the mighty men are broken,”

The song turns to a series of reversals. “The bows of the mighty men are broken.” Warriors who relied on their weapons find them shattered. The bow was the long-range weapon of the strongest armies.

“And those who stumbled are girded with strength.”

Those who “stumbled,” the weak and faltering, are “girded with strength,” clothed with strength as with a belt. The first of the song's reversals shows that human strength does not decide who stands. God breaks the strong and strengthens the weak. This pattern will appear throughout 1 Samuel, from the defeat of Israel's army when it trusted the ark (4:10) to David's victory over Goliath (17:47).

reflections.title: Strength You Put On
reflections.html: “The bows of the mighty men are broken, and those who stumbled are girded with strength.” “Girded” means to tie on, like a belt: strength here is not grown from within but fastened on from outside. The verb “broken” is used for the breaking of people, not just objects; the warriors are shattered inwardly, not merely disarmed. Every power determined to be something in itself is broken, and every weakness that despairs of itself is turned into power. “My strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). The stumbling believer is not disqualified; he is the one God dresses for battle.
reflections.q: “The bows of the mighty men are broken, and those who stumbled are girded with strength.”

reflections.title: The Great Reversal of Human Strength
reflections.html: Here begins one of Scripture’s central motifs: God loves to dismantle human self-sufficiency while empowering human weakness. He breaks the bow of the strong because they rely on it; He girds the stumbler because the stumbler relies on Him. Natural strength must be broken before spiritual strength can be bound on, for God cannot use our self-sufficiency. Hannah moves here from a domestic dispute to military imagery, and the reversal she sings will run through Eli’s fall and Samuel’s rise, Saul’s fall and David’s rise. God delights to use the overlooked and the sidelined. Verses 4–7 hold seven such contrasts: mighty and stumbling, full and hungry, barren and fruitful, killing and making alive, bringing down and bringing up, poor and rich, low and lifted.
reflections.q: Here begins one of Scripture’s central motifs: God loves to dismantle human self-sufficiency while empowering human weakness.

reflections.title: The Bow Broken at the Cross
reflections.html: At the cross the ultimate “bow of the mighty,” the power of Satan, was broken, and feeble humanity, through faith, was girded with resurrection life (Colossians 2:15).
reflections.q: At the cross the ultimate “bow of the mighty,” the power of Satan, was broken, and feeble humanity, through faith, was girded with resurrection life (Colossians 2:15).

5.brief: Those who were full must hire themselves out for bread while the hungry are satisfied, and the barren woman bears seven while the mother of many grows feeble. Hannah sets her own story within a wider pattern of God reversing human conditions, with seven expressing complete blessing.
5.explain:
“Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread,”

The reversals continue in daily life. Those who once had plenty must now work for food. “Hired themselves out” describes the humiliation of the formerly well-off who must labor for a meal.

“And the hungry have ceased to hunger.”

Meanwhile, “the hungry,” the poor and needy, are satisfied. Mary echoes this line: “He has filled the hungry with good things, And the rich He has sent away empty” (Luke 1:53).

“Even the barren has borne seven,”

Now Hannah's own story appears in the pattern. “The barren has borne seven.” “Seven” expresses complete and abundant blessing. Hannah would eventually bear six children (Samuel and five more, 2:21), so the number speaks of fullness rather than an exact count.

“And she who has many children has become feeble.”

The mother of many “has become feeble,” grown weak and forlorn. The line recalls Peninnah, though the song does not name her. Hannah sets her own story within a wider pattern of God reversing human conditions. Her personal experience becomes a testimony to how God works with all people.
5.notes: Ruth 4:15 likewise uses “seven sons” as a comparison expressing abundance.

reflections.title: The Barren Has Borne Seven
reflections.html: “Even the barren has borne seven, and she who has many children has become feeble.” When Hannah sang this she had one son; she would eventually have six children in all (v. 21). Seven is the number of full blessing and divine completion (Ruth 4:15), so she is not counting; she is confessing what God does. Her faith spoke of God’s fullness before she could see it in her own home, and in God’s eyes she was already complete. Her song reached beyond her own life to the fruitfulness of every spiritually barren soul who trusts God, a hope sung again in Psalm 113:9 and Isaiah 54:1, applied to the church in Galatians 4:27, and echoed in Mary’s Magnificat. The same God who fills the empty can empty the full; Jeremiah later turns the picture to judgment: “She who has borne seven has languished” (Jeremiah 15:9). Faith learns to speak of His fullness before the house is full.
reflections.q: “Even the barren has borne seven, and she who has many children has become feeble.”

reflections.title: Never Trust in Abundance
reflections.html: “Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have ceased to hunger.” The well-fed are reduced to day labor. God delights in overturning human systems of security. Never place ultimate trust in material abundance; it is entirely subject to divine sovereignty. This very line will be fulfilled before the chapter ends, when Eli’s well-fed house begs for bread (v. 36). (An old Jewish legend said that for every child Hannah bore, Peninnah buried two; that is legend, not text.)
reflections.q: “Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have ceased to hunger.”

6.brief: The LORD kills and makes alive; He brings down to the grave and brings up. Life and death themselves lie under His authority.
6.explain:
“The LORD kills and makes alive;”

Hannah's song now reaches the most basic reversal: life and death. “The LORD kills and makes alive.” He holds authority over both. Moses sang the same truth: “I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39). No power in heaven or earth shares that authority.

“He brings down to the grave and brings up.”

“The grave” translates the Hebrew word Sheol, the realm of the dead. God “brings down” to it and “brings up” from it. Life and death themselves lie under His authority. The line may describe God's power to restore those near death, as He had brought new life out of Hannah's barren womb. In the light of the whole Bible, it also anticipates God's power to raise the dead.
6.notes: In the Old Testament, Sheol, the Hebrew word translated “the grave” in this verse, is the place or state of the dead. Being brought up from Sheol can describe rescue from mortal danger, as when the psalmist says, “You brought my soul up from the grave” (Psalm 30:3).

reflections.title: The God Who Brings Up From Sheol
reflections.html: “The LORD kills and makes alive; He brings down to the grave and brings up.” Hannah is quoting the Song of Moses: “I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39). Her womb had been a kind of grave, and God had brought life out of it. Long before the resurrection was fully revealed, the Spirit moved a praying mother to declare God’s power over the grave, a striking flash of resurrection faith before any resurrection had been recorded. The full answer stands at the end of the story: the Son was brought down to death and brought up again (Psalm 16:10; Acts 2:27–32), securing eternal life for all who are united with Him, and He says, “I have the keys of Hades and of Death” (Revelation 1:18). The God of Hannah’s song is the God of the empty tomb. No grave is final when the God of Hannah holds it.
reflections.q: “The LORD kills and makes alive; He brings down to the grave and brings up.”

reflections.title: The Descent Is in His Hand Too
reflections.html: No second cause is final; life and death are finally in God’s hand alone. For the believer walking through a “down” season, the comfort is precise: the descent is within His hand too, and the God who brings down is the God who brings up.
reflections.q: No second cause is final; life and death are finally in God’s hand alone.

7.brief: The LORD makes poor and makes rich; He brings low and lifts up. Wealth and status are not finally in human hands but under His rule.
7.explain:
“The LORD makes poor and makes rich;”

The reversals extend to wealth. “The LORD makes poor and makes rich.” Riches and poverty are not finally determined by human effort or luck, but by God's hand.

“He brings low and lifts up.”

The summary line states the pattern of the whole song and of the whole book: “He brings low and lifts up.” Wealth and status are not finally in human hands but under His rule. In 1 Samuel this pattern will unfold in history: Eli's house brought low and Samuel raised up, Saul brought low and David raised up. The line also anticipates the larger biblical pattern seen supremely in Christ, who humbled Himself and was highly exalted (Philippians 2:8–9).
7.notes: Psalm 75:7 uses similar wording: “He puts down one, And exalts another.”

reflections.title: Both Seasons Come From One Hand
reflections.html: “The LORD makes poor and makes rich; He brings low and lifts up.” Hannah had been told twice that “the LORD had closed her womb” (1:5–6). She does not credit her low years to Peninnah, Elkanah, or fate, nor her lifting to her own persistence. Both seasons came from the same hand. Wealth, poverty, promotion, and demotion are under God’s purposeful administration. This verse overturns both the prosperity mindset (wealth proves God’s favor) and the self-made mindset (wealth proves my effort); it destroys the illusion of the self-made person and comforts the downtrodden. Station and circumstance are assignments, not verdicts on our worth. Perhaps God makes some poor because they could not bear riches without ruin. A believer who sees both the valley and the lifting as coming from his Father’s hand can be humble when lifted and hopeful when brought low.
reflections.q: “The LORD makes poor and makes rich; He brings low and lifts up.”

reflections.title: The Curriculum of the Present Season
reflections.html: Accept your present station, abundance or lack, as God’s current curriculum for your soul. God allows seasons of plenty and seasons of want for His purposes; our part is to obey Him and leave the consequences to Him. True spiritual wealth often requires the stripping away of riches we made ourselves.
reflections.q: Accept your present station, abundance or lack, as God’s current curriculum for your soul.

8.brief: God raises the poor from the dust and the beggar from the ash heap to seat them among princes and give them a throne of glory. He has every right to do this, because the pillars of the earth belong to Him and He has set the world upon them.
8.explain:
“He raises the poor from the dust And lifts the beggar from the ash heap,”

God lifts the lowest. “The dust” and “the ash heap” picture the place of the most destitute, the garbage mound outside a town where outcasts sat. Psalm 113 uses almost the same words (Psalm 113:7–8).

“To set them among princes And make them inherit the throne of glory.”

God raises the poor not merely to survival but to honor. He seats them “among princes” and gives them “the throne of glory,” a seat of honor. The reversal is complete: from the ash heap to the throne.

“For the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, And He has set the world upon them.”

The reason God can do this is that He owns and governs the world. “The pillars of the earth” is a poetic picture of the earth's foundations (compare Psalm 75:3; Job 38:4–6). The Creator who set the world on its foundations has every right to rearrange human fortunes as He wills.
8.notes: “Glory” translates the Hebrew word kavod. It belongs to a Hebrew word group whose basic idea is weight or heaviness, and which also means honor. The same word group becomes significant later in these chapters: Eli honors his sons above God (2:29–30), and Ichabod's name declares that the glory has departed (4:21–22).

reflections.title: From the Ash Heap to the Throne of Glory
reflections.html: “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the beggar from the ash heap, to set them among princes and make them inherit the throne of glory.” The ash heap was the town’s refuse pile, where outcasts sat and begged, the place Job ended up (Job 2:8; Lamentations 4:5). “Throne of glory” is kisse’ kabod, literally a “seat of weight.” Eli sat on his seat (kisse’) and would fall from it because he was “heavy” (kabed, 4:18); Hannah sings that God hands the seat of weight to beggars. God does not merely improve a beggar’s condition in the ash heap; He changes his citizenship and seats him with royalty. God bypasses the self-righteous and goes to the ash heap of humanity to find His kings and priests. That is the exact path of a sinner saved by grace: raised from the dirt of spiritual death and made to “sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6). God’s honor does not go to those who sit heavily in religious places; it goes to those He lifts from the dust.
reflections.q: “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the beggar from the ash heap, to set them among princes and make them inherit the throne of glory.”

reflections.title: The Transfer of the Ash Heap
reflections.html: How does God lift us from the ash heap? Read through the lens of Christ, the answer is staggering. Jesus, the Prince of heaven, voluntarily left His seat of honor and came down to sit on the ash heap of humanity (Philippians 2:6–8): born in a borrowed stable, crucified outside the city. The great reversal of Hannah’s song is possible only because of the great exchange of the cross. We get the seat of honor because Christ took the ash heap.
reflections.q: How does God lift us from the ash heap?

reflections.title: God Does Not Reform the Ash Heap
reflections.html: A powerful evangelistic text: God does not reform the ash heap; He removes the beggar from it and seats him with royalty. His grace reaches the lowest point of society to lift to the highest point of heaven.
reflections.q: A powerful evangelistic text: God does not reform the ash heap; He removes the beggar from it and seats him with royalty.

reflections.title: Inherited, Not Earned
reflections.html: “And make them inherit the throne of glory.” The beggar does not climb to the throne or buy his seat; he inherits it, the way a child receives an estate. An inheritance belongs to children and comes as a father’s gift. Every verb in the verse is God’s: He raises, lifts, sets, and makes them inherit. The honor of God’s people is not a promotion we work toward but an inheritance we receive as sons and daughters (Romans 8:17; Revelation 3:21).
reflections.q: “And make them inherit the throne of glory.”

reflections.title: The Pillars of the Earth
reflections.html: “For the pillars of the earth are the LORD’s, and He has set the world upon them.” The line grounds God’s right to reverse human fortunes in His ownership of the world itself. The God who holds up the foundations of the earth is more than able to manage the affairs of one barren woman’s household, and to lift one beggar. (The first lines of the verse return almost word for word in Psalm 113:7–8, and Mary echoes the reversal in Luke 1:52.)
reflections.q: “For the pillars of the earth are the LORD’s, and He has set the world upon them.”

9.brief: The LORD guards the feet of His saints, while the wicked are silenced in darkness. The verse states the song’s conclusion plainly: no one prevails by his own strength.
9.explain:
“He will guard the feet of His saints,”

God protects His faithful people. “Saints” translates a word meaning those who are loyal to Him, the godly who live by His faithful love. “Guard the feet” pictures God keeping them from stumbling along the way (compare Psalm 91:11–12).

“But the wicked shall be silent in darkness.”

The wicked come to the opposite end. “Silent in darkness” pictures defeat and death. Those who talked proudly (2:3) are finally silenced.

“For by strength no man shall prevail.”

The verse states the song's conclusion plainly: “by strength no man shall prevail.” No one succeeds by his own power. The truth Hannah learned in her barrenness applies to warriors, kings, and nations. It will be repeated in David's words to Goliath, “the LORD does not save with sword and spear; for the battle is the LORD's” (17:47).
9.notes:
“Saints” translates the Hebrew hasidim, ‘faithful’ or ‘godly ones.’ The word is related to hesed, God's steadfast, faithful love, and describes people who show that same loyal love toward Him. Hannah's song promises that God guards those who belong to Him in this way.

The written Hebrew text has the singular ‘His saint,’ while the traditional reading has the plural, which the NKJV follows.

reflections.title: He Guards the Feet
reflections.html: “He will guard the feet of His saints.” “Guard” is the keeping word of Psalm 121, to guard as a watchman guards: “He will not allow your foot to be moved; He who keeps you will not slumber” (Psalm 121:3). “Saints” are the chasidim, those bound to Him by His covenant love (chesed). If God keeps their feet, how much more their heads and hearts. He keeps them from falling, from wandering, from wounds, from the net. The believer’s safety lies not in the firmness of his own step but in the faithfulness of the One who keeps it. In this chapter a heavy priest will one day fall from his seat (4:18), while a small boy is kept upright in a corrupt house. We are “kept by the power of God” (1 Peter 1:5), and Christ is our preserver; we do not maintain our salvation by our might but by His guarding of our steps. “Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling” (Jude 24) is the New Testament form of Hannah’s confidence.
reflections.q: “He will guard the feet of His saints.”

reflections.title: Not by Strength
reflections.html: “For by strength no man shall prevail.” This is one of the Old Testament’s clearest declarations of grace over works. Hannah did not overcome Peninnah by out-arguing or out-producing her; she prevailed by pouring out her soul before the LORD. Human strength, intellect, and willpower always fail in the final spiritual contest; prevailing is God’s keeping power, not human exertion. A few verses later a priest’s servant will say, “If not, I will take it by force” (v. 16); the song has already passed sentence on that method. “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). Stop striving in the flesh. In God’s house, force is a sign of weakness, and dependence is the real strength.
reflections.q: “For by strength no man shall prevail.”

reflections.title: Silent in Darkness
reflections.html: “The wicked shall be silent in darkness.” The wicked are struck speechless, cut off, when God withdraws the light of His grace. The mouths that talked so proudly (v. 3) end in silence.
reflections.q: “The wicked shall be silent in darkness.”

10.brief: The LORD will break His adversaries, thunder against them from heaven, and judge the ends of the earth, and He will give strength to His king and exalt the horn of His anointed. Spoken before Israel had a king, these closing words are prophetic, anticipating the kings Samuel will anoint and, in the wider canon, the Messiah.
10.explain:
“The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken in pieces;”

The song moves toward its climax. “The adversaries of the LORD” are those who oppose Him, and they will be shattered.

“From heaven He will thunder against them.”

God will “thunder” from heaven against His enemies. The image of God's thunder appears in David's song (Psalm 18:13) and will be fulfilled literally later in 1 Samuel, when “the LORD thundered with a loud thunder upon the Philistines” at Mizpah (7:10).

“The LORD will judge the ends of the earth.”

God's judgment reaches “the ends of the earth.” Hannah's vision has grown from her own household to the whole world.

“He will give strength to His king,”

Now comes a remarkable line. God “will give strength to His king.” When Hannah spoke these words, Israel had no king. The people were still governed by judges, and the demand for a king lay years in the future (8:5). Kingship was anticipated in the Law (Deuteronomy 17:14–15), but Hannah speaks of “His king,” the king God Himself would provide.

“And exalt the horn of His anointed.”

The song ends with the LORD exalting “the horn of His anointed.” “His anointed” refers to the one God sets apart by anointing for His service, here the king. The Hebrew word is mashiach, from which comes ‘Messiah.’ The horn image returns from 2:1: as God exalted Hannah's horn, He will exalt the horn of His anointed king. Spoken before Israel had a king, these closing words are prophetic. Hannah's son Samuel would later anoint both Saul and David. In the wider canon, the line looks beyond them to the Messiah. Zacharias praised God for raising up “a horn of salvation for us In the house of His servant David” (Luke 1:69).

Hannah's song reaches far beyond her personal circumstances. The woman who prayed for a son now speaks of God's king and His anointed. This is consistent with the understanding that her prayer at Shiloh became an encounter with God's purposes for Israel, and that she perceived something of what He was doing through the son she had given Him.
10.notes:
This is the first time in Scripture that the Hebrew word mashiach, ‘anointed,’ is applied to a king; earlier it describes the anointed priest (Leviticus 4:3). The same word lies behind “My anointed” in 2:35, and it is the source of the English word ‘Messiah.’

Hannah's “His king” differs from Israel's later demand for a king “like all the nations” (8:5, 20).

The books of Samuel open with Hannah's song about God's king and anointed and close with David's song about God's deliverance of His king and anointed (2 Samuel 22:51).

reflections.title: Grace Was the First to Say “His Anointed”
reflections.html: “He will give strength to His king, and exalt the horn of His anointed.” Israel had no king when Hannah sang, nor any human movement yet asking for one. Earlier Scripture had spoken of an anointed priest (Leviticus 4:3), but here, for the first time, mashiach, “anointed,” names a king, an exalted, conquering royal figure. The Greek Old Testament translated it “His Christ,” and even a medieval rabbi admitted that the King of whom Hannah speaks is the Messiah. Her song reaches past Samuel to David, and past David to Christ. The woman whose name means “grace” was the first to give the coming King His title. The Holy Spirit was speaking of Jesus through the lips of a praying mother, and the last word of her song is the first word of a hope that ends in Jesus the Christ.
reflections.q: “He will give strength to His king, and exalt the horn of His anointed.”

reflections.title: Suffering Became the Lens
reflections.html: Out of the crucible of her personal barrenness, Hannah’s spiritual vision was cracked wide open to see the ultimate King. Deep personal suffering, brought to the Lord, often becomes the very lens through which God grants revelation of His larger redemptive plan.
reflections.q: Out of the crucible of her personal barrenness, Hannah’s spiritual vision was cracked wide open to see the ultimate King.

reflections.title: Her Son Would Carry the Horn
reflections.html: “And exalt the horn of His anointed.” Hannah sang of the anointed’s horn as a figure of speech. Years later her son would hear, “Fill your horn with oil,” and “Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed” David (16:1, 13). The boy she left at Shiloh became the man who poured the horn over the head of the king she had seen in her song. A mother’s Spirit-given praise became her son’s assignment. What God speaks into a praying parent’s heart can become the life’s work of the child.
reflections.q: “And exalt the horn of His anointed.”

reflections.title: The Song Begins and Ends With a Lifted Horn
reflections.html: “Exalt the horn of His anointed” answers “my horn is exalted” in verse 1: the song begins with Hannah lifted and ends with the King lifted. One woman’s answered prayer becomes a window into God’s plan for the world. Zacharias calls Jesus “a horn of salvation … in the house of His servant David” (Luke 1:69). Our enemy is broken because the Anointed One’s horn has been exalted. (The thunder from heaven is fulfilled at Mizpah, 7:10, and in the harvest storm, 12:18.)
reflections.q: “Exalt the horn of His anointed” answers “my horn is exalted” in verse 1: the song begins with Hannah lifted and ends with the King lifted.
