11.brief: Elkanah returns home to Ramah, but the child remains and ministers to the LORD before Eli the priest. The song gives way to the narrative, and Samuel’s service is introduced before the account of Eli’s sons begins.
11.explain:
“Then Elkanah went to his house at Ramah.”

The song gives way to narrative. Elkanah returned home to “Ramah.” Hannah went with him, as 2:19 shows.

“But the child ministered to the LORD before Eli the priest.”

Samuel stayed. “The child ministered to the LORD.” “Ministered” describes serving at the sanctuary as an attendant, a word used of priests and Levites. Samuel's service was “to the LORD,” while he was “before Eli the priest,” under Eli's supervision. Samuel's service is introduced before the account of Eli's sons begins, so that the reader sees the faithful child first. The narrative will now alternate between Samuel's service and the sons' corruption.
11.notes:
Chapter 2 alternates between Eli's sons (2:12–17, 22–25) and Samuel (2:11, 18–21, 26).

The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads that Hannah ‘left him there before the Lord, and departed to Armathaim,’ that is, to Ramah. The Hebrew text followed by the NKJV says instead that Elkanah went to his house at Ramah.

reflections.title: Elkanah Went Home; the Boy Stayed
reflections.html: “Then Elkanah went to his house at Ramah. But the child ministered to the LORD before Eli the priest.” One short verse splits the family with a single “but.” The parents walk home, less than a day’s journey, to a house with one child fewer. The Greek Old Testament adds, “and she left him there before the LORD.” Having received the very thing she wept to obtain, Hannah surrendered it at once. The vow was not finished in the song but in the walk home. Real surrender includes the quiet trip back to an emptier house, and God sees that walk as clearly as He heard the song. True maturity is being as faithful to God in the fulfillment of the promise as we were in the agonizing wait for it.
reflections.q: “Then Elkanah went to his house at Ramah.

reflections.title: A Child’s Ministry Is Real Ministry
reflections.html: “The child ministered to the LORD.” The verb (sharat) is the official word for the service of priests and Levites and of Joshua’s service to Moses (Exodus 24:13); it means the willing service of a free person, not the labor of a slave, and certainly not babysitting. A small boy may have lit lamps, carried vessels, and opened doors (3:15). He served “to the LORD” and “before Eli”: by obeying the old priest he was serving God. Children in God’s house are not waiting to begin ministry later; small tasks done to the LORD are ministry now. Churches should treat children as real participants in worship.
reflections.q: “The child ministered to the LORD.”

reflections.title: Ministry to the Lord Comes First
reflections.html: Before Samuel ever ministered to the people, he ministered to the LORD, and that order shaped his whole life. Ministry to the Lord is the highest calling, and every servant must remember that ministry begins as service to God before it is service to others. In the same verse the narrative sets the purity of the child against the corruption about to be exposed.
reflections.q: Before Samuel ever ministered to the people, he ministered to the LORD, and that order shaped his whole life.

12.brief: The narrator states plainly that Eli’s sons were corrupt and did not know the LORD. Though they held priestly office, they had no true knowledge of the God they were appointed to serve.
12.explain:
“Now the sons of Eli were corrupt;”

The narrator states plainly what Eli's sons were. “Corrupt” translates the Hebrew ‘sons of Belial,’ meaning worthless, wicked men. The same expression appeared when Hannah begged Eli not to regard her as ‘a daughter of Belial’ (1:16). Eli had suspected the godly woman of worthlessness, while his own sons were the worthless ones.

“they did not know the LORD.”

The deeper problem is stated next: “they did not know the LORD.” They held priestly office, wore the priestly garments, and handled the sacrifices, but they had no true knowledge of the God they were appointed to serve. To “know the LORD” in Scripture means more than knowing facts about Him; it means a relationship of loyalty, reverence, and obedience. After Joshua's generation died, Judges says, “another generation arose after them who did not know the LORD” (Judges 2:10). Eli's sons belonged to that kind of generation, even at the altar.
12.notes:
The Hebrew behind “corrupt” is ‘sons of beliyya'al,’ literally ‘sons of worthlessness,’ a phrase for the lawless and worthless (Deuteronomy 13:13; Judges 19:22). The NKJV's “corrupt” captures the sense.

Samuel also “did not yet know the LORD” in 3:7, but the reason is different. Samuel had not yet received the LORD's word; Eli's sons rejected the LORD in their conduct.

reflections.title: The Tragedy of Proximity Without Intimacy
reflections.html: “Now the sons of Eli were worthless men; they did not know the LORD.” Hophni and Phinehas grew up in the tabernacle. They were born into the priesthood, handled the holy vessels daily, breathed the incense, and ate the sacrifices. They knew all about the LORD, yet they did not know Him. “Know” (yada’) is the word of relationship and experience, not information; the Targum renders it, “did not know to fear before the LORD.” Proximity to the things of God does not equal intimacy with the Person of God. Religious familiarity without personal surrender produces the most dangerous kind of spiritual blindness. It is entirely possible to make a career of the holy while remaining spiritually dead, and spiritual pedigree and religious vocation do not equal a relationship with God. Here is a terrifying warning to all raised in the faith or serving in ministry: unregenerate people can hold professional positions in God’s house.
reflections.q: “Now the sons of Eli were worthless men; they did not know the LORD.”

reflections.title: “Not” and “Not Yet”
reflections.html: In the next chapter the narrator says, “Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD” (3:7). The difference is one small word. The priests’ sons had handled the altar, the meat, and the incense for years and did not know Him; the boy who was only beginning to serve did not know Him yet. A man who holds a sacred office and is presumed to know the Lord, but does not, stands where blessing hardly reaches him. Nearness to holy things is not the same as knowing the Holy One, and the person who still says “not yet” is closer than the one who has stopped asking. Are we closer to “not” or to “not yet”?

reflections.title: A Sentence That Implicates the Father
reflections.html: The Hebrew is a verbless clause: literally, “The sons of Eli, sons of Belial.” The wording can be heard as setting Eli beside Belial, a quiet hint that the father shares the guilt, which the man of God will make plain in verse 29. “Belial” means “without profit,” worthless, good for nothing, and by Paul’s day it had become a name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). The Greek Old Testament calls them “pests” or “plagues,” men dangerous to everyone around them. Hannah had once begged Eli not to count her “a daughter of Belial” (1:16); the true sons of Belial were his own. Being related to a high priest is no substitute for a relationship with God. A godly family name can sit on top of a worthless life, and a father’s position cannot cover a son’s heart. “Because you have rejected knowledge, I also will reject you from being priest for Me” (Hosea 4:6).
reflections.q: The Hebrew is a verbless clause: literally, “The sons of Eli, sons of Belial.”

13.brief: The priests had made their own custom: while a worshiper’s sacrifice was boiling, the priest’s servant came with a three-pronged fleshhook. Their practice replaced the portion God had prescribed with a system that served their own appetite.
13.explain:
“And the priests' custom with the people was that when any man offered a sacrifice,”

The narrator describes the priests' practice. “Custom” translates a word that often means ‘judgment’ or ‘ordinance.’ The priests had established their own rule for dealing with the people's sacrifices, replacing what God had commanded. The sacrifices in view were peace offerings, shared between the altar, the priest, and the worshiper's family.

“the priest's servant would come with a three-pronged fleshhook in his hand while the meat was boiling.”

While the worshiper's meat was boiling, “the priest's servant would come with a three-pronged fleshhook,” a large fork for lifting meat from a pot. The Law assigned the priest specific portions, the breast and the right thigh (Leviticus 7:31–34). These priests ignored that portion and sent their servants to grab whatever they could. Their practice replaced the portion God had prescribed with a system that served their own appetite.
13.notes:
Leviticus 7:31–34 gave the priests the breast and the right thigh of peace offerings. Deuteronomy 18:3 lists the shoulder, cheeks, and stomach.

“Custom” translates the Hebrew word mishpat, which usually means judgment or justice but can also mean a right, a due, or a customary practice. It may also be read with the end of verse 12: ‘they did not know the LORD, nor the priests' due from the people.’ Some translations adopt that division.

reflections.title: The Custom That Replaced the Command
reflections.html: “The priests’ custom with the people was that when any man offered a sacrifice, the priest’s servant would come with a three-pronged fleshhook in his hand while the meat was boiling.” “Custom” is mishpat, the word for justice, judgment, and ordinance. The priests had an ordinance, and it was a fork. They wrote their own law. God had already set the priests’ share, the breast and right thigh of the peace offering, after the fat was burned (Leviticus 7:30–34). The fork was an innovation of greed, designed to grab more than God allotted. When leadership loses the fear of God, it begins to exploit the flock and builds self-serving systems to extract what belongs to God and to the people. When leaders turn their appetites into policy, people stop calling it sin and start calling it the way things are done. Every church practice needs to be measured again against the Word that first defined it. Where have our preferences quietly become “the way we’ve always done it,” serving us more than honoring God?
reflections.q: serving us more than honoring God?

reflections.title: Stabbing Into the Fellowship Meal
reflections.html: The offering in view is the peace offering, the only sacrifice in which the worshiper ate a share; his portion was boiling for his family’s meal when the servant arrived with the fork. (The word for the three-pronged fork occurs only here and in verse 14.)
reflections.q: The offering in view is the peace offering, the only sacrifice in which the worshiper ate a share; his portion was boiling for his family’s meal when the servant arrived with the fork. (The word for the three-pronged fork occurs only here and in verse 14.)

14.brief: The servant thrust the fleshhook into the pot, and the priest kept whatever it brought up, and this was done to every Israelite who came to Shiloh. The abuse was not occasional but the standard treatment of all who came to worship.
14.explain:
“Then he would thrust it into the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot;”

The servant “would thrust” the fork into whatever vessel was being used. The list of four cooking vessels shows that no pot was safe from the priests' fork.

“and the priest would take for himself all that the fleshhook brought up.”

Whatever the fork brought up, the priest kept. The amount depended on chance and greed, not on God's command.

“So they did in Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there.”

The abuse was not occasional. “So they did in Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there.” It was the standard treatment of every worshiper. Elkanah's family, coming up year after year to worship (1:3, 21), would have experienced it. Every Israelite who came to Shiloh to meet God met corrupt priests at the altar.

reflections.title: Every Pot in Shiloh
reflections.html: “Then he would thrust it into the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot; and the priest would take for himself all that the fleshhook brought up. So they did in Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there.” The narrator names four different cooking vessels, as if to say that no family’s pot was safe. The priest’s share was decided by what the prongs happened to catch, not by what God had assigned. They monetized the worship of God. It was done “to all the Israelites,” rich and poor alike, and the yearly meal at which Elkanah handed portions to his family (1:4) took place in this same courtyard. Corruption at the center of worship reaches every household that comes to worship.
reflections.q: “Then he would thrust it into the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot; and the priest would take for himself all that the fleshhook brought up.

15.brief: Even before the fat was burned, the servant demanded raw meat for the priest to roast. The fat belonged to the LORD and was to be burned first, so the priests were taking their share ahead of God’s.
15.explain:
“Also, before they burned the fat,”

The abuse went further. The Law required that the fat of the peace offering be burned on the altar first, because “all the fat is the LORD's” (Leviticus 3:16). The fat was God's portion and was to be offered before anyone else ate.

“the priest's servant would come and say to the man who sacrificed,”

Before the fat was burned, the servant came and made demands of the worshiper.

“Give meat for roasting to the priest, for he will not take boiled meat from you, but raw.”

The servant demanded raw meat, which the priest preferred to roast. The fat belonged to the LORD and was to be burned first, so the priests were taking their share ahead of God's. They put their own appetite before the LORD's portion. This was not a minor breach of etiquette. It was taking what belonged to God and treating His offering as theirs.
15.notes: Leviticus 7:31 adds that the priest “shall burn the fat on the altar, but the breast shall be Aaron's and his sons'.” Eli's sons reversed that order.

reflections.title: Served Before God Was Served
reflections.html: “Also, before they burned the fat, the priest’s servant would come and say, ‘Give meat for roasting to the priest, for he will not take boiled meat from you, but raw.’” The law was plain: “all the fat is the LORD’s” (Leviticus 3:16), and the priest’s portion came only after the fat had burned on the altar (Leviticus 7:30–31). The word “also” marks the worst of the crimes: this was robbery of God. They would serve themselves before God was served; they would have God wait on them rather than wait on God. The issue was not hunger but order. Whatever we take before God has received His portion, we have placed above Him. Does God receive our firstfruits, our first hours, first dollars, first affections, or whatever is left over?
reflections.q: Does God receive our firstfruits, our first hours, first dollars, first affections, or whatever is left over?

reflections.title: The Flesh Hates the Altar’s Fire
reflections.html: The fat was the Lord’s portion, meant to be consumed by the fire on the altar, and the priests wanted the meat before the fire touched it. Unredeemed flesh always hates the altar’s fire. It wants the blessing, the sustenance, and the prestige without passing through the purifying flames of consecration.
reflections.q: The fat was the Lord’s portion, meant to be consumed by the fire on the altar, and the priests wanted the meat before the fire touched it.

reflections.title: Raw, “Living” Meat
reflections.html: “Raw” is literally “living” meat. Roasting was specified in the law for the Passover lamb, not for the priest’s share, and raw meat let the priests pick the best cuts, perhaps even to sell them. Both practices, the fork and the raw-meat demand, stand condemned.
reflections.q: “Raw” is literally “living” meat.

16.brief: When a worshiper urged that the fat be burned first, the servant refused and threatened to take the meat by force. Worshipers who wanted to honor the LORD were overruled and intimidated by the very men who should have led them.
16.explain:
“And if the man said to him, ‘They should really burn the fat first;’”

Some worshipers objected. They knew the Law and wanted the fat burned first, as God required. “They should really burn the fat first” shows a worshiper trying to honor God.

“then you may take as much as your heart desires,”

The worshiper even offered the priest as much as he wanted afterward. He was not being stingy; he simply wanted God honored first.

“he would then answer him, ‘No, but you must give it now; and if not, I will take it by force.’”

The servant refused and threatened violence: “if not, I will take it by force.” Worshipers who wanted to honor the LORD were overruled and intimidated by the very men who should have led them. The priests' servants acted like robbers at the altar.

reflections.title: The Worshiper Who Corrected the Priest
reflections.html: “If the man said, ‘They should really burn the fat first; then you may take as much as your heart desires.’” An ordinary worshiper pleads for God’s portion while offering to give up his own. What a shame that priests needed to be reminded of their duty by the people; the worshipers were more righteous than the priests, more concerned for God’s honor than the men at the altar. Sometimes the clearest voice for God in the courtyard belongs to the person with no title. Leaders should listen when the people they serve say, “God first,” and every believer can be that voice, even when no one in charge wants to hear it.
reflections.q: “If the man said, ‘They should really burn the fat first; then you may take as much as your heart desires.’”

reflections.title: Ministry That Bullies Is Not Ministry
reflections.html: “No, but you must give it now; and if not, I will take it by force.” The priest’s servant threatens a worshiper at God’s altar. Coercion had entered the house of God. Hannah had just sung, “By strength no man shall prevail” (v. 9). The law said of the peace offering, “his own hands shall bring” it (Leviticus 7:30); force tears from a worshiper’s hands what he came to give. Position and sacred office never excuse abuse, and God’s people should recognize spiritual bullying for what it is. Authority in God’s house that needs force to get its way has already lost its authority. Elders are to serve “not as being lords over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3).
reflections.q: “No, but you must give it now; and if not, I will take it by force.”

17.brief: The sin of the young men was very great before the LORD, because the LORD’s offering was treated with contempt. The priests themselves despised God’s offering, and their conduct also damaged the people’s regard for worship.
17.explain:
“Therefore the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD,”

The narrator gives God's verdict. “The sin of the young men was very great before the LORD.” “Young men” refers to Eli's sons, and possibly their servants. Their sin was “before the LORD,” committed in His presence and seen by Him. It was “very great,” not a small lapse.

“for men abhorred the offering of the LORD.”

The reason is that “men abhorred the offering of the LORD.” “Abhorred” means to treat with contempt or scorn. “The offering of the LORD” was the sacrifice brought to Him. The Hebrew wording allows two dimensions. The priests themselves treated God's offering with contempt, which the immediate context strongly supports. Their conduct also damaged the people's regard for worship, as worshipers who saw the priests' greed came to despise the offering itself. Both dimensions belong to the seriousness of their sin.
17.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “men” is general, and the verb can be read as describing the priests' own contempt or the effect of their conduct on others.

The context, especially 2:29 (“Why do you kick at My sacrifice and My offering”), supports the priests' contempt as primary, though the question is not conclusively settled.

A Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel and the Septuagint lack the word “men,” reading ‘they treated the offering of the LORD with contempt,’ which makes the priests the subject.

reflections.title: Sin That Gave Worship a Bad Name
reflections.html: “Therefore the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD, for men abhorred the offering of the LORD.” The verb means to treat with contempt, and it can be read as causative: the priests caused the offering to be despised. The worshipers themselves came to look down on the offerings because of what they saw. The most devastating consequence of their sin was not their own defilement but that ordinary Israelites learned to despise the things of God (compare Romans 2:24; 2 Samuel 12:14). People stop coming where their consciences have been wounded. And note “before the LORD”: what worshipers endured in the courtyard, God saw from the throne. When leaders abuse authority, they do catastrophic collateral damage to the faith of the people they were ordained to serve. A leader’s sin is measured not only by what it takes but by whom it drives away from God. Has anything in our leadership, parenting, or example made it harder for someone to love worshiping God?
reflections.q: Has anything in our leadership, parenting, or example made it harder for someone to love worshiping God?

reflections.title: Familiarity Breeds a Deadly Contempt
reflections.html: Familiarity with holy things can breed a deadly, casual contempt. Manipulating the things of God to serve personal appetite invites severe judgment. The theft of meat was small compared with the contempt for worship it spread among the people.
reflections.q: Familiarity with holy things can breed a deadly, casual contempt.

18.brief: In contrast, Samuel ministers before the LORD even as a child, wearing a linen ephod. The boy serves faithfully in the same sanctuary where the priests are corrupt.
18.explain:
“But Samuel ministered before the LORD,”

The narrative turns back to Samuel in sharp contrast. “But Samuel ministered before the LORD.” In the same sanctuary where the priests were corrupt, the boy served faithfully. “Before the LORD” describes his service as offered in God's presence.

“even as a child,”

“Even as a child” emphasizes his youth. The narrator uses the same word for Samuel (“child”) that he used for Eli's sons (“young men”) in 2:17. The two kinds of young men stand side by side.

“wearing a linen ephod.”

Samuel wore “a linen ephod,” a simple garment worn by those serving at the sanctuary. The high priest wore a more elaborate ephod (Exodus 28:4), but simple linen ephods were worn by other priests (22:18) and by David when he danced before the ark (2 Samuel 6:14). Samuel's ephod marked him as set apart for the LORD's service.
18.notes:
The ephod was a garment worn over the upper body. The high priest's ephod was richly made of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet (Exodus 28:6).

The linen ephod was a simpler garment associated with sanctuary service. Wearing it did not make Samuel an Aaronic priest.

reflections.title: A White Flower on a Dunghill
reflections.html: “But Samuel ministered before the LORD, even as a child, wearing a linen ephod.” The narrator cuts from the fork in the pot to a child in a linen garment with a single “but,” and that word is a hinge. Samuel at Shiloh was like a white flower blooming on a dunghill, and Hannah had just sung that God lifts the beggar “from the ash heap” (v. 8). Amid gross sexual and financial corruption at the highest levels of spiritual leadership, God was quietly raising up a pure servant. Samuel was not removed from the corruption of Shiloh; he was kept pure inside it, his mother’s prayers around him like a wall of fire. Jesus prayed for His disciples in the same way: “not that You should take them out of the world, but that You should keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). Samuel is a beautiful type of Christ, the faithful Son who ministers in spotless righteousness whatever the corruption around Him.
reflections.q: “But Samuel ministered before the LORD, even as a child, wearing a linen ephod.”

reflections.title: Never Underestimate God’s “But”
reflections.html: While the old order was rotting, God was already clothing His answer. The plain linen ephod was a simple priestly garment, worn later by David before the ark (2 Samuel 6:14) and by the priests of Nob (22:18). Samuel, a Levite by descent though not of Aaron’s line (1 Chronicles 6), was by God’s providence clothed in priestly linen, quietly displacing Eli’s sons. In dark seasons God is often preparing a “but.” In a season when the glory seems to have departed from something we care about, are we looking for the quiet “but Samuel” God may be raising up?
reflections.q: God may be raising up?

reflections.title: From “Before Eli” to “Before the LORD”
reflections.html: In verse 11 Samuel “ministered to the LORD before Eli the priest”; in verse 18 he “ministered before the LORD,” literally “before the face of the LORD.” The change marks growth: the boy who began under a human supervisor is now described as serving in God’s own presence. Faithful service under human oversight is the doorway into service consciously before God Himself. The goal of every mentor, as Eli in this one respect understood, is to bring a young servant to the place where he serves before the Lord and not merely before people.
reflections.q: In verse 11 Samuel “ministered to the LORD before Eli the priest”; in verse 18 he “ministered before the LORD,” literally “before the face of the LORD.”

reflections.title: Clothed in His Linen
reflections.html: Christ is our true Priest, and we, as God’s children, are clothed in the linen of His righteousness, ministering in the temple of His Spirit (Revelation 19:8).
reflections.q: Christ is our true Priest, and we, as God’s children, are clothed in the linen of His righteousness, ministering in the temple of His Spirit (Revelation 19:8).

19.brief: Each year Hannah makes Samuel a little robe and brings it to him when she comes up with her husband for the yearly sacrifice. Her care for her son continues even after she has given him to the LORD.
19.explain:
“Moreover his mother used to make him a little robe,”

Hannah's care for her son continued. Each year she made him “a little robe,” a small outer garment sized for the growing boy. The word is the same used for the high priest's robe (Exodus 28:31) and later for Samuel's robe (15:27; 28:14) and Saul's robe (24:4).

“and bring it to him year by year when she came up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.”

She brought it “year by year” when the family came up for “the yearly sacrifice.” Her care for her son continued even after she had given him to the LORD. Each robe was a little larger than the last, measuring the years. Hannah had given Samuel to the LORD for life, but she did not stop loving him or caring for him. Giving him to God did not end her motherhood.
19.notes: The Hebrew word for “robe” here recurs at several points in 1 Samuel: Hannah's little robe for Samuel (2:19), the torn robe when Saul is rejected (15:27), Jonathan's robe given to David (18:4), the corner of Saul's robe cut by David (24:4, 11), and the robe (NKJV “mantle”) by which Saul recognizes Samuel from the woman's description (28:14).

reflections.title: A Robe That Grew With Him
reflections.html: “Moreover his mother used to make him a little robe, and bring it to him year by year.” A boy grows, so each year’s robe had to be larger than the last. Hannah sewed by memory and estimate, measuring a son she saw once a year; only someone who was there would think to record such a detail. She could not keep Samuel, but she could clothe him. She did not abandon him; she nurtured his calling from a distance, stitching his growth into the garments she made. Surrender to God did not end a mother’s love; it turned it into faithful, yearly, mostly unseen acts. Giving a child to God does not mean letting go of caring for him; it means caring in a new way, releasing control while never ceasing to invest, visit, and pray.
reflections.q: “Moreover his mother used to make him a little robe, and bring it to him year by year.”

reflections.title: The Woven Garment of Hidden Preparation
reflections.html: This little robe is a picture of incremental, hidden growth. Spiritual maturity is not handed over overnight. It is woven year by year through small acts of faithfulness, quiet devotion, and an expanding capacity to carry the presence of God. We cannot wear tomorrow’s mantle today; we must grow into our calling season by season.
reflections.q: This little robe is a picture of incremental, hidden growth.

reflections.title: The Mother’s Ministry of the Robe
reflections.html: The robe is a picture of intercession. Hannah kept fashioning a covering for her son as he grew. So do the unseen, continual prayers of intercessors and parents who pray coverings over the next generation of spiritual leaders: love woven in secret and carried to the house of God. What hidden act of love can we keep carrying to God for someone we have entrusted to Him?
reflections.q: What hidden act of love can we keep carrying to God for someone we have entrusted to Him?

reflections.title: Parents Are Always Sewing Little Coats
reflections.html: Habits are the clothing of the soul, and parents are always making little coats their children will wear long after any fabric would have worn out. Paul uses clothing language for character: “put on tender mercies, kindness, humility, meekness, longsuffering” (Colossians 3:12). Habits are sewn not mainly in crises but in daily things: how parents speak to each other, how they spend their time, how they pray. Every home is a workroom where children’s inner garments are being made, for better or worse. What little coats are we sewing by our habits, our speech, and our prayer?
reflections.q: What little coats are we sewing by our habits, our speech, and our prayer?

reflections.title: The Robe Comes Back
reflections.html: “Robe” is me’il, the word for the high priest’s robe (Exodus 28:31), and it follows Samuel through the book. When Saul seized the edge of his robe and it tore, Samuel said, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today” (15:27–28). Even at Endor, Samuel is recognized as “an old man … covered with a mantle,” a me’il (28:14). The garment a mother first sewed for a small boy became the identifying garment of the prophet’s life. What parents begin in love can mark their child’s calling to the very end.
reflections.q: “Robe” is me’il, the word for the high priest’s robe (Exodus 28:31), and it follows Samuel through the book.

20.brief: Eli blesses Elkanah and his wife, asking the LORD to give them descendants in place of the son given to the LORD, and they return home. The priest’s blessing honors the gift Hannah has made.
20.explain:
“And Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, and say,”

Each year Eli blessed the couple. The priest who once misjudged Hannah now regularly blessed her household.

“The LORD give you descendants from this woman for the loan that was given to the LORD.”

Eli asked the LORD to give them “descendants from this woman,” more children from Hannah, “for the loan that was given to the LORD,” in place of Samuel, whom they had given to God. “Loan” uses the same root as ‘ask’ and ‘lent’ in 1:27–28. The priest's blessing honored the gift Hannah had made.

“Then they would go to their own home.”

The family returned home each year, leaving Samuel at Shiloh.
20.notes:
The Hebrew reads literally ‘for the request which he asked of the LORD,’ using ‘he’ rather than ‘she.’ That is awkward, since Hannah was the one who asked; ‘he’ may refer to Elkanah as the head of the family.

The Septuagint has Eli speak to the parents directly. Brenton's English translation of the Septuagint reads ‘the loan which thou hast lent to the Lord,’ using the older English ‘thou’ for ‘you.’ Several modern translations make Hannah the one who gave, as the ESV does with ‘for the petition she asked of the LORD.’ The NKJV's “for the loan that was given to the LORD” captures the sense without deciding who gave.

reflections.title: Eli Could Bless Other Homes
reflections.html: “And Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, and say, ‘The LORD give you descendants from this woman for the loan that was given to the LORD.’” The priest whose own house was collapsing still spoke blessing over another family, year after year, and the next verse shows that God honored his words (v. 21). His blessing was not an empty wish. God often honors the office of spiritual authority and the faith of those who receive, even when the vessel dispensing the blessing is badly flawed; His grace is not handcuffed by the weakness of His ministers. Yet Eli could pronounce good over Elkanah’s household while failing to bring order to his own. “If a man does not know how to rule his own house, how will he take care of the church of God?” (1 Timothy 3:5).
reflections.q: “And Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, and say, ‘The LORD give you descendants from this woman for the loan that was given to the LORD.’”

reflections.title: What Is Lent to the LORD Is Never Lost
reflections.html: “The loan that was given to the LORD” repeats the wordplay of 1:27–28: the verb “ask” or “lend” echoes in the names Samuel and Saul. We can never out-give God. This is not a formula for getting a return; it is a revelation of His generous character. What we surrender fully to God, He answers with His own kindness, and often multiplies back in greater measure.
reflections.q: “The loan that was given to the LORD” repeats the wordplay of 1:27–28: the verb “ask” or “lend” echoes in the names Samuel and Saul.

21.brief: The LORD visits Hannah, and she bears three sons and two daughters, while the child Samuel grows before the LORD. God answers with generous fruitfulness, and Samuel’s growth continues in His presence.
21.explain:
“And the LORD visited Hannah,”

The LORD answered Eli's blessing. “Visited” means God came to act on her behalf, as when “the LORD visited Sarah” and gave her Isaac (Genesis 21:1).

“so that she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters.”

Hannah bore “three sons and two daughters.” God answered with generous fruitfulness. The woman who had given her only son received five more children. Her song had said, “the barren has borne seven” (2:5), and here God filled her home.

“Meanwhile the child Samuel grew before the LORD.”

The verse closes by returning to Samuel. “The child Samuel grew before the LORD.” He was growing up in God's presence. The phrase “before the LORD” recurs in Samuel's story (2:18, 21), marking his life as lived in God's sight.

reflections.title: God Is No Man’s Debtor
reflections.html: “And the LORD visited Hannah, so that she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters.” Hannah gave God one son; God gave her five more children. Whatever is wholly consecrated to God is never truly lost. God will not be out-given; the surrender of an Isaac or the dedication of a Samuel always meets a multiplied return of grace, grace upon grace (John 1:16). And the “seven” of her song became reality in fullness. The Woman of Grace received five more children.
reflections.q: “And the LORD visited Hannah, so that she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters.”

reflections.title: Visited Like Sarah
reflections.html: “Visited” (paqad) is the verb of Genesis 21:1, “the LORD visited Sarah as He had said,” and of Exodus 4:31, when Israel learned God had visited them in Egypt. It means to attend to closely and act; Ruth 1:6 uses it when “the LORD had visited His people by giving them bread.” Hannah stands in the line of barren mothers God visited: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson’s mother. God’s visit is covenant attention, not a casual call. When God visits, He does not drop by; He comes with His purpose in His hands.
reflections.q: “Visited” (paqad) is the verb of Genesis 21:1, “the LORD visited Sarah as He had said,” and of Exodus 4:31, when Israel learned God had visited them in Egypt.

reflections.title: Grew Up With God
reflections.html: “Meanwhile the child Samuel grew before the LORD,” or literally, “grew up with the LORD,” near Him and under His care. While Hannah’s house in Ramah filled with five more children, her firstborn grew up with God as his household. The same verb is used of Moses, who also grew up away from his mother (Exodus 2:10). Growth “before the LORD” is the only kind that lasts; Samuel’s roots went down into the soil of the sanctuary itself. While Eli’s sons withered in the same courtyard, Samuel flourished: the environment was identical; the orientation of the heart was different. So the life of Christ within us grows as we abide continually in His presence, untouched by surrounding corruption. The child given away was not lost; he grew up in the closest company there is.
reflections.q: “Meanwhile the child Samuel grew before the LORD,” or literally, “grew up with the LORD,” near Him and under His care.

22.brief: Eli, now very old, hears everything his sons are doing to all Israel, including lying with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting. Their corruption extends beyond seizing the offerings to sexual immorality at the place of worship.
22.explain:
“Now Eli was very old;”

The narrative turns back to Eli's house. “Eli was very old.” He was approaching ninety-eight, his age at death (4:15). His age may help explain his weakness, but it does not excuse it.

“and he heard everything his sons did to all Israel,”

Eli “heard everything his sons did.” He was not ignorant of their behavior. Their abuses affected “all Israel,” since worshipers came to Shiloh from throughout the nation.

“and how they lay with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting.”

Their corruption went beyond seizing offerings. They “lay with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting.” These women served at the entrance of the sanctuary, as women had done since the wilderness (Exodus 38:8). Eli's sons used their priestly position for sexual immorality at the very place of worship. Such conduct resembled the practices of Canaanite religion, which Israel was commanded to reject.
22.notes:
Exodus 38:8 mentions “the serving women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting,” whose bronze mirrors were used for the laver. Their duties are not described, but they evidently served at the sanctuary entrance.

The clause about the women is absent from the Septuagint. The chapter's other evidence of the sons' corruption does not depend on it.

reflections.title: Defiling the Women Who Came to Serve
reflections.html: “And how they lay with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting.” The phrase repeats Exodus 38:8 almost word for word, where the bronze laver was made “from the bronze mirrors of the serving women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting.” Those women gave up their mirrors so priests could wash before serving. Here priests who should have washed at that laver defiled the women who came to serve. “Assembled” is the root of “hosts,” a word for enlisted, organized service; service at the tent was a kind of spiritual warfare. The sons made the tabernacle a place where sin was committed rather than confessed, mixing pure worship with the gross immorality of pagan fertility rites Israel was meant to reject. Leaders who prey on the devoted commit a double sin, against the person and against the house of God, and desecrate the most precious thing in it: people who came to serve Him. The church must protect the vulnerable, not the reputation of the powerful.
reflections.q: “And how they lay with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting.”

reflections.title: Sin at the Very Door
reflections.html: The enemy’s greatest triumph is not bringing sin into the world but bringing it to the very door of the sanctuary. It reveals a seared conscience when men can move seamlessly from offering sacrifices to gross immorality in the same place.
reflections.q: The enemy’s greatest triumph is not bringing sin into the world but bringing it to the very door of the sanctuary.

reflections.title: Phinehas at the Door Again
reflections.html: Eli named his son after Phinehas son of Eleazar, the zealous priest who stopped Israel’s immorality at Shittim while the people wept “at the door of the tabernacle of meeting” (Numbers 25:6), and who received “a covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was zealous for his God” (Numbers 25:13). The second Phinehas did at the door of the tabernacle what the first Phinehas had executed men for. The name carried the zeal; the man carried the opposite. A godly name does not make a godly heart, and a family’s spiritual heritage can be spent in a single generation.
reflections.q: Eli named his son after Phinehas son of Eleazar, the zealous priest who stopped Israel’s immorality at Shittim while the people wept “at the door of the tabernacle of meeting” (Numbers 25:6), and who received “a covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was zealous for his God” (Numbers 25:13).

reflections.title: Knowing Is Not the Same as Acting
reflections.html: “Now Eli was very old, and he heard everything his sons did.” Eli was near ninety (he died at ninety-eight, 4:15), and he was not ignorant; he heard everything, again and again. He was a passive father and a permissive priest. Delayed obedience is disobedience, and information without action only increases accountability. What do we already know about sin in our lives, families, or ministries that we have addressed only with words and never with action?
reflections.q: What do we already know about sin in our lives, families, or ministries that we have addressed only with words and never with action?

23.brief: Eli confronts his sons, asking why they do such things, since he hears of their evil dealings from all the people. Their wickedness has become public knowledge throughout Israel.
23.explain:
“So he said to them, ‘Why do you do such things?’”

Eli confronted his sons. “Why do you do such things?” is a rebuke, not a request for information. Eli knew what they were doing.

“For I hear of your evil dealings from all the people.”

He told them that their “evil dealings” were known to “all the people.” Their wickedness had become public knowledge throughout Israel. The sons' sins were not secret, and they were damaging the reputation of the LORD's sanctuary.

reflections.title: A Question Where a Command Was Needed
reflections.html: “So he said to them, ‘Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all the people.’” Eli asks why. The question was understandable but needless, because no good reason could exist. As father, high priest, and judge, Eli had authority to remove his sons from service (Deuteronomy 17:12; 21:18–21), and he asked them a question instead. His rebuke used the language of mild disappointment rather than the language of righteous authority, far too gentle for the size of the offense. In leadership and parenting, soft rebukes for hard sins do not produce repentance; they communicate complicity. Words without action told his sons everything they needed to know about how seriously he meant it. Some situations do not need another question; they need a decision. Love that only asks “Why?” when it should say “No more” leaves the sinner in charge.
reflections.q: “So he said to them, ‘Why do you do such things?

reflections.title: Reputation Instead of Righteousness
reflections.html: Eli’s appeal rests on what people are saying: “I hear of your evil dealings from all the people … it is not a good report.” He seems more concerned with the report spreading among the people than with the holiness of God being violated. The rebuke was general, framed as a question, and based on hearsay he had not troubled to examine. Correction built on reputation teaches children to hide sin, not to hate it. The question that changes a heart is not “What are people saying?” but “What does God see?” (Compare David with Adonijah: “his father had not rebuked him at any time by saying, ‘Why have you done so?’” 1 Kings 1:6.)
reflections.q: Eli’s appeal rests on what people are saying: “I hear of your evil dealings from all the people … it is not a good report.”

24.brief: Eli tells his sons that the report he hears is not good and that they are making the LORD’s people transgress. Their sin harms not only themselves but leads God’s people into wrongdoing.
24.explain:
“No, my sons!”

Eli's rebuke continued with an emotional appeal. “No, my sons!” expresses both his authority as their father and his distress.

“For it is not a good report that I hear.”

“Not a good report” is an understatement. The reports were shameful.

“You make the LORD's people transgress.”

Eli named the gravest consequence: “You make the LORD's people transgress.” Their sin harmed not only themselves but led God's people into wrongdoing. By abusing the sacrifices, they caused worshipers to despise the offering (2:17). By their immorality at the sanctuary, they corrupted the worship of Israel. Priests who should have led the people to God were leading them away from Him.
24.notes: “You make the LORD's people transgress” can also be translated ‘the LORD's people are spreading it about,’ referring to the report. The NKJV follows the traditional rendering; the ESV and NRSV have ‘spreading abroad.’

reflections.title: Right Diagnosis, No Treatment
reflections.html: “No, my sons! For it is not a good report that I hear. You make the LORD’s people transgress.” Eli named the true weight of the sin: his sons were causing God’s people to cross a line. His diagnosis was correct and his treatment was missing. What he said was right, but it was not enough. It is possible to fall into grave sin by thinking it very important to be nice to people. Knowing exactly how serious a sin is and still speaking softly about it is a deeper failure than ignorance. (Note the tender “my sons” here against the man of God’s “your sons” in verse 29.)
reflections.q: “No, my sons!

25.brief: Eli warns that God may judge when one person wrongs another, but asks who will intercede for a man who sins against the LORD, exposing how grave his sons’ offense has become. They do not heed their father, because the LORD desired to kill them, a judgment on their persistent rebellion that does not remove their responsibility.
25.explain:
“If one man sins against another, God will judge him.”

Eli explained why their sin was so serious. When “one man sins against another,” there is someone to judge between them. “God will judge him” may mean that God will arbitrate, or that God's appointed judges will settle the matter. Human wrongs can be addressed.

“But if a man sins against the LORD, who will intercede for him?”

But when “a man sins against the LORD,” who can stand between him and God? The sons' sin was directly against God, in His sanctuary, with His offerings. If the priests, who were supposed to intercede for others, sinned against God Himself, who would intercede for them? The question exposes how grave their offense had become.

“Nevertheless they did not heed the voice of their father,”

The sons ignored the warning. “They did not heed the voice of their father.” Eli's words had no effect.

“because the LORD desired to kill them.”

The narrator gives the reason in startling terms: “because the LORD desired to kill them.” God had determined to judge them. This statement must be understood alongside their persistent rebellion and refusal to heed correction. The LORD's judicial decision did not force innocent or willing men into sin; it confirmed the course they had chosen. Their responsibility remains fully theirs. At the same time, the text plainly states God's sovereign judgment, and that statement should not be weakened. A point can come when persistent rebellion meets the settled judgment of God (compare Proverbs 29:1).
25.notes: The Hebrew word Elohim can refer to God or, in some legal contexts, to human judges acting for God (Exodus 21:6; 22:8, where the NKJV translates “the judges”).

reflections.title: Who Will Intercede?
reflections.html: “If one man sins against another, God will judge him. But if a man sins against the LORD, who will intercede for him?” There is a wordplay here: “judge” and “intercede” both come from palal, the verb used when Hannah “prayed” (1:10; 2:1), the root of the common Hebrew word for prayer. When people wrong each other, God can stand between them as judge; when a man wrongs God, who can stand between? This is one of the most terrifying questions in the Old Testament, and Eli asked it as if there were no answer. He identified the fatal problem of the old order: no human third party has the standing to mediate between God and a man who has offended God, and the Law had no remedy for high-handed rebellion against Yahweh Himself but death. This verse cries out for the incarnation. What was a rhetorical dead end in the Old Testament becomes the bedrock of the New. Here the lid comes off the Tupperware: Jesus Christ, the God-Man, holding the hand of the offended God and the hand of the offending man, is the very Intercessor Eli thought impossible to find. “There is one God and one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). “If anyone sins, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1–2), and “He always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25). The most hopeless question in the chapter has its answer in Christ. Do we live daily in the relief that Jesus answers Eli’s question?
reflections.q: Do we live daily in the relief that Jesus answers Eli’s question?

reflections.title: When God Decides
reflections.html: “Nevertheless they did not heed the voice of their father, because the LORD desired to kill them.” “Desired” is the word God uses in Ezekiel: “I have no pleasure in the death of one who dies” (Ezekiel 18:32; 33:11). The two statements are not in conflict. God takes no pleasure in the death of sinners, yet after long, persistent, high-handed rebellion He may reach a point of judicial decision, confirming the heart’s chosen direction (Romans 1:24), as with Pharaoh, whose heart was hardened both by himself and by God. Their sins were capital offenses under the law (Leviticus 7:25; 22:9). Because they had continually rejected Him, God withdrew the grace of repentance and sealed their rebellion toward judgment; their refusal to listen was the seal of what was coming. God can will a hardening without being the author of evil. There is a “too late” no one can locate in advance, and so the call is to turn while God’s voice still pleads (Hebrews 3:15). God’s goodness gives long warning; it does not give endless permission. Are we presuming on His patience as if opportunities to repent will never run out?
reflections.q: Are we presuming on His patience as if opportunities to repent will never run out?

reflections.title: Sovereignty and Responsibility in One Verse
reflections.html: Verse 25 declares both that the sons “did not heed” and that “the LORD desired to kill them.” Scripture never asks us to choose between human guilt and divine sovereignty: their rebellion was fully their own; God’s judgment was fully His. The verse also answers an unspoken question. God did not tolerate their abuse because He was indifferent; He had already determined its end.
reflections.q: Verse 25 declares both that the sons “did not heed” and that “the LORD desired to kill them.”

26.brief: Meanwhile the child Samuel grows in stature and in favor with both the LORD and men. His steady growth stands in sharp contrast to the hardening of Eli’s sons, and Luke describes the boy Jesus in nearly the same words (Luke 2:52), pointing ahead to the Son who would please His Father fully.
26.explain:
“And the child Samuel grew in stature,”

In contrast to Eli's sons, “the child Samuel grew.” He grew “in stature,” physically maturing as a boy.

“and in favor both with the LORD and men.”

He also grew “in favor both with the LORD and men.” God was pleased with him, and people recognized his character. His steady growth stands in sharp contrast to the hardening of Eli's sons. They were rejected by God and despised by the people (2:17, 23–24); Samuel was favored by both.

Luke describes the boy Jesus in nearly the same words: “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men” (Luke 2:52). The echo places Samuel's faithful growth alongside the growth of the Son who would please His Father fully.

reflections.title: Growing Both Ways at Once
reflections.html: “And the child Samuel grew in stature, and in favor both with the LORD and men.” The Hebrew reads literally “went on growing, and good,” and the verse stands in brilliant contrast to the darkening doom of Eli’s house. Luke borrows this sentence for Jesus: “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men” (Luke 2:52). Samuel is set up as a type of Christ, the faithful one growing against the dark backdrop of a corrupt religious system. Samuel is a faithful servant who grows in a corrupt temple; Jesus is the Son who grows up to cleanse the temple and become its replacement (John 2:19–21). Favor with God and favor with people are not rivals; in Samuel and supremely in Jesus they grew together. Spiritual health needs vertical growth and horizontal grace. A young person who grows toward God does not need to grow away from others to do it.
reflections.q: “And the child Samuel grew in stature, and in favor both with the LORD and men.”

reflections.title: Grow in Favor With God First
reflections.html: The growth is Godward and manward, but in that order. Favor with people that is not rooted in favor with God is fragile; favor with God will eventually shape a life others recognize as good. (The verb can also mean “became great,” fitting what Samuel became, 3:19–20.)
reflections.q: The growth is Godward and manward, but in that order.

27.brief: A man of God comes to Eli with the word of the LORD, who reminds Eli that He clearly revealed Himself to his father’s house when they were in Egypt under Pharaoh. The message of judgment begins by recalling the LORD’s gracious initiative toward Eli’s family.
27.explain:
“Then a man of God came to Eli and said to him,”

An unnamed prophet now confronts Eli. “A man of God” was a title for a prophet, someone who spoke for God (compare Deuteronomy 33:1; 1 Samuel 9:6). His name is not given; his message is what matters.

“Thus says the LORD:”

The prophet speaks with God's authority. “Thus says the LORD” introduces a message from God Himself, not the man's opinion.

“Did I not clearly reveal Myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt in Pharaoh's house?”

The message begins by recalling God's gracious initiative. “The house of your father” refers to Eli's ancestral family, the house of Aaron and the tribe of Levi. God says He did “clearly reveal” Himself to them “when they were in Egypt.” He spoke to Aaron in Egypt and called him to stand with Moses (Exodus 4:14, 27). The message of judgment begins by recalling the LORD's gracious initiative toward Eli's family. Everything they had came from God's grace.
27.notes:
1 Samuel does not trace Eli's genealogy. Later texts place Abiathar, Eli's descendant, in the line of Ithamar, Aaron's younger son (compare 1 Chronicles 24:3, 6). The judgment on Eli's house concerns this branch of the priesthood, not the whole line of Aaron.

The title “man of God” is used of Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), the angel who appeared to Manoah's wife (Judges 13:6), and Samuel (9:6–10).

reflections.title: A Nameless Man of God
reflections.html: “Then a man of God came to Eli and said to him, ‘Thus says the LORD.’” He has no name, no hometown, and no further role. He appears, speaks, and disappears; the message matters more than the messenger. In a time when “the word of the LORD was rare” (3:1), God bypassed the high priest’s own office and sent His word from outside it. When leadership will not correct itself, God raises outside voices to speak. When God sends a message, it matters little who brings it. His word does not need a famous mouth; it needs a faithful one, and the most important messages sometimes come through people we would never have chosen.
reflections.q: “Then a man of God came to Eli and said to him, ‘Thus says the LORD.’”

reflections.title: Judgment Begins With Grace Remembered
reflections.html: “Did I not clearly reveal Myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt in Pharaoh’s house?” The rebuke does not begin with Eli’s sin but with God’s self-revelation to Aaron in Egypt (Exodus 4:14, 27), a question Eli could only answer with a silent yes. God grounds His judgment in the grace He had shown Aaron’s house, which makes Eli’s failure a betrayal of grace, not merely of law. Before He says “you kicked,” He says, “I revealed Myself, I chose, I gave” (vv. 27–28). Sin looks most serious when it is seen against grace. God’s judgments on His people often begin by recounting His unmerited favor, and His correction always begins by reminding them who He has been to them.
reflections.q: “Did I not clearly reveal Myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt in Pharaoh’s house?”

28.brief: The LORD recalls that He chose Eli’s ancestral house out of all the tribes of Israel to be His priests, to offer at His altar, burn incense, and wear the ephod before Him, and that He gave them the offerings made by fire. The priesthood was a privilege God had granted, together with His provision for them.
28.explain:
“Did I not choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be My priest,”

God reminds Eli that He “chose” his ancestor “out of all the tribes of Israel to be My priest.” The priesthood was not earned or inherited by right; it was God's choice (Exodus 28:1).

“to offer upon My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod before Me?”

God lists the priest's privileges: “to offer upon My altar,” “to burn incense” (Exodus 30:7–8), and “to wear an ephod before Me.” Each was a sacred duty performed in God's presence.

“And did I not give to the house of your father all the offerings of the children of Israel made by fire?”

God had also provided for the priests. He gave them “all the offerings of the children of Israel made by fire,” their share of the sacrifices (Leviticus 7:35–36; Numbers 18:8). The priesthood was a privilege God had granted, together with His provision for them. Eli's sons had no need to steal; God had already given them more than enough.

reflections.title: Three Privileges at the Center of Worship
reflections.html: “Did I not choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be My priest, to offer upon My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod before Me?” The priest was first “My priest,” God’s before he was the people’s. Each privilege put him at the center of Israel’s meeting with God: the altar (atonement and access), the incense (prayer rising before God, Psalm 141:2), and the ephod, whose shoulder stones carried the names of Israel’s tribes before the LORD “as a memorial” (Exodus 28:12), and which held the means of seeking God’s guidance. Every privilege of nearness was given for God and for others. Eli’s house turned privileges into perks. Every believer is now part of “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), and the same temptation and the same calling apply.
reflections.q: “Did I not choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be My priest, to offer upon My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod before Me?”

reflections.title: Greater Privilege, Greater Accountability
reflections.html: God also gave the priests “all the offerings made by fire,” their inheritance in place of land (Deuteronomy 18:1; Numbers 18:8–20). They had plenty and still grabbed for more, which made the theft inexcusable. The higher the privilege and the deeper the grace given to a family or a leader, the stricter the accountability when that privilege is abused. “To whom much is given, from him much will be required” (Luke 12:48).
reflections.q: God also gave the priests “all the offerings made by fire,” their inheritance in place of land (Deuteronomy 18:1; Numbers 18:8–20).

reflections.title: The Boy Already Wore What They Were Losing
reflections.html: The house chosen “to wear an ephod before Me” is about to lose its place, while a few verses earlier a boy was already ministering before the LORD “wearing a linen ephod” (v. 18). God had dressed the replacement before the sentence was read. He prepares His answer before He announces His judgment. Nothing God removes leaves Him without a servant.
reflections.q: The house chosen “to wear an ephod before Me” is about to lose its place, while a few verses earlier a boy was already ministering before the LORD “wearing a linen ephod” (v. 18).

29.brief: The LORD asks why Eli’s house kicks at His sacrifice and offering, and He charges Eli with honoring his sons more than Him and with sharing in the best of the offerings they took from Israel. Eli has given his sons the honor that belongs to God and has grown fat on what they seized.
29.explain:
“Why do you kick at My sacrifice and My offering which I have commanded in My dwelling place,”

Now comes the charge. “Why do you kick at My sacrifice and My offering?” “Kick” pictures an animal kicking back in defiance. Moses used the same image for Israel: “Jeshurun grew fat and kicked” (Deuteronomy 32:15). The offerings were ones God had “commanded in My dwelling place.” By treating them with contempt, the priests were kicking against God Himself.

“and honor your sons more than Me,”

The charge falls on Eli personally: God accuses him of choosing to “honor your sons more than Me.” “Honor” comes from the root meaning ‘weight’ or ‘glory.’ Eli gave his sons more weight than God by allowing them to continue their abuses rather than removing them from office. His fatherly attachment outweighed his duty to God.

“to make yourselves fat with the best of all the offerings of Israel My people?”

The plural “yourselves” includes Eli. He had shared in the best of the offerings that his sons seized. Eli had given his sons the honor that belonged to God and had grown fat on what they took. Later the narrator notes that Eli was “heavy” when he fell and died (4:18), using the same root as “honor.”
29.notes:
In Hebrew, “honor” in this verse, “heavy” in 4:18, and “glory” in 4:21–22 all come from the same word group, built on the idea of weight. The repetition links Eli's honoring of his sons above God with his own death and with the departure of the glory from Israel.

The Hebrew behind “kick at” is unusual here. The Septuagint and a Hebrew manuscript of Samuel from Qumran read instead ‘why do you look with a greedy eye,’ a reading followed by the RSV and NRSV. The NKJV's “kick” follows the traditional Hebrew text, and the same Hebrew verb is used in Deuteronomy 32:15, where Israel “grew fat and kicked.”

reflections.title: Kicking Like a Fattened Ox
reflections.html: “Why do you kick at My sacrifice and My offering which I have commanded in My dwelling place?” “Kick” appears only twice in the Old Testament: here and in the Song of Moses, “But Jeshurun grew fat and kicked … and scornfully esteemed the Rock of his salvation” (Deuteronomy 32:15). Picture an overfed ox that becomes unmanageable and refuses its kind master. The danger in God’s house was not hunger but fullness. And the sin was committed in God’s own dwelling place, His home. Well-fed people are in the most danger of kicking at the God who fed them.
reflections.q: “Why do you kick at My sacrifice and My offering which I have commanded in My dwelling place?”

reflections.title: Silence Is a Way of Honoring
reflections.html: “And honor your sons more than Me, to make yourselves fat with the best of all the offerings of Israel My people.” Eli never stole meat with a fork; he simply did not stop the men who did. God calls that “honoring” his sons above Him. “Honor” is kabed, to give weight. Those who do not use their authority to restrain their children in effect honor them more than God. And the plural “yourselves” includes Eli: he was eating what his sons had stolen, sharing the plate, and he would later die because he was “heavy” (4:18). God’s glory had been stolen and wrapped around Eli’s belly. He gave weight to the wrong things and became weighty in the wrong way. Whatever we will not confront in those we love, we have made heavier than God.
reflections.q: “And honor your sons more than Me, to make yourselves fat with the best of all the offerings of Israel My people.”

reflections.title: The Idolatry of Family
reflections.html: God diagnoses the root of Eli’s passive leadership. It was not merely weakness; it was idolatry. By refusing to remove his sons from office to protect God’s holiness, Eli effectively worshiped his children above his Creator. Idolatry is often found in raising legitimate loves above the supreme love. Whenever we tolerate sin in our loved ones at the expense of God’s honor, we have made idols of them. Whom or what have we honored above God, a child, a relationship, a career, our comfort?
reflections.q: Whom or what have we honored above God, a child, a relationship, a career, our comfort?

30.brief: The LORD had said that Eli’s house would walk before Him forever, but now He declares, “Far be it from Me.” His principle governs the outcome, “those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed,” so the earlier word does not secure an unfaithful family’s privileged place.
30.explain:
“Therefore the LORD God of Israel says: ‘I said indeed that your house and the house of your father would walk before Me forever.’”

God recalls His earlier promise. He had said that the priestly house “would walk before Me forever.” The Law had said of Aaron's sons, “The priesthood shall be theirs for a perpetual statute” (Exodus 29:9). “Walk before Me” describes faithful service in God's presence.

“But now the LORD says: ‘Far be it from Me;’”

God now says, “Far be it from Me.” He will not continue this privilege for Eli's house.

“for those who honor Me I will honor,”

God states the principle: “those who honor Me I will honor.” Those who give God His proper weight will receive honor from Him.

“and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed.”

The reverse is also true: “those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed.” “Lightly esteemed” is the opposite of ‘heavy’ or ‘honored,’ meaning treated as of little weight. God's principle governs the outcome, so the earlier word did not secure an unfaithful family's privileged place. God's promise concerning priestly service did not guarantee that an unfaithful branch would keep its office regardless of its conduct. God remained faithful to His purposes for the priesthood as a whole, but He would not honor those who despised Him.
30.notes: In Hebrew, “honor” and “lightly esteemed” are opposites: the first comes from the idea of weight, the second from the idea of being light or of little account.

reflections.title: Honor Has Weight; Contempt Has None
reflections.html: “For those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed.” This is the moral center of the chapter. “Honor” is kabed, to make heavy, give weight; “lightly esteemed” is qalal, to be light, trifling. To honor God is to give Him weight: first place, first portion, true reverence. To despise Him is to treat Him as light, and God will make us light. God does not merely observe this; He responds to it. People who give God weight are given weight; people who treat Him as light become light. If Eli had honored God in his household, God would have honored his family. This is not a reward formula but a description of how the God of glory relates to people, an unshakable law of the spiritual universe. While salvation is by unconditional grace, divine honor and usefulness in ministry are bound up with our reverence for God. He will strip the influence from anyone who handles His glory lightly. What would it look like for us to give God weight this week?
reflections.q: What would it look like for us to give God weight this week?

reflections.title: The Runner Who Gave God Weight
reflections.html: Eric Liddell famously received this verse on a slip of paper at the 1924 Paris Olympics after refusing to run on the Lord’s Day, and then won the 400 meters. Accounts differ on how he received the note, but the verse found a man who had already decided whom he would honor.
reflections.q: Eric Liddell famously received this verse on a slip of paper at the 1924 Paris Olympics after refusing to run on the Lord’s Day, and then won the 400 meters.

reflections.title: A Promise Is Not a Permit
reflections.html: “I said indeed that your house and the house of your father would walk before Me forever.’ But now the LORD says: ‘Far be it from Me.’” God had promised the priesthood to Aaron’s line “by a perpetual statute” (Exodus 29:9; Numbers 25:13). “Far be it from Me” comes from a root meaning “to profane”: it would be a profane thing to Me to keep such men walking before Me. God does not revoke His promise to Aaron’s priesthood; He rejects a false trust that treats the promise as protection for unholy men. God’s promise to Aaron was enduring, but the participation of Eli’s particular line depended on faithfulness. The promise of priesthood was never a license for irreverence. No inherited privilege can shield anyone from God’s holiness (Matthew 3:9). Are we treating a privilege, position, or spiritual heritage as a permanent pass rather than a stewardship?
reflections.q: Are we treating a privilege, position, or spiritual heritage as a permanent pass rather than a stewardship?

31.brief: The LORD announces that days are coming when He will cut off the arm, the strength, of Eli and his father’s house, so that no man in his house will reach old age. The family that fattened itself on the offerings will be weakened and cut short.
31.explain:
“Behold, the days are coming that I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father's house,”

God announces judgment. “The days are coming” points to a future time. “I will cut off your arm” means God will break the strength of Eli's family. “Arm” is a common image for strength and power.

“so that there will not be an old man in your house.”

The specific judgment is that no man in Eli's house would live to old age. “There will not be an old man in your house.” Eli himself lived to ninety-eight (4:15), but his descendants would die young. The family that fattened itself on the offerings would be weakened and cut short.
31.notes: The deaths of Hophni and Phinehas in battle (4:11), the slaughter of the priests at Nob (22:17–19), and the removal of Abiathar (1 Kings 2:27) record the judgment unfolding over generations.

reflections.title: No Old Man in the House of an Old Man
reflections.html: “Behold, the days are coming that I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will not be an old man in your house.” This is said to a man the narrator has just called “very old” (v. 22). Eli’s long life had not been used to restrain evil; age made him cool and slack in his duty rather than wise. Now no one in his line would reach the age he had wasted. Long life is God’s gift for faithful use, not a guarantee that faithfulness can be postponed.
reflections.q: “Behold, the days are coming that I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will not be an old man in your house.”

reflections.title: Cutting Off the Arm
reflections.html: The “arm” is strength, influence, and authority. When a spiritual house loses its reverence, it inevitably loses its spiritual authority. It may keep a title, but it will lose the arm of God’s power.
reflections.q: The “arm” is strength, influence, and authority.

reflections.title: Arms Cut Off Like Dagon’s
reflections.html: “I will cut off your arm” uses an image found nowhere else in the Old Testament, and it is acted out literally three chapters later, when the idol Dagon is found fallen before the ark with “both the palms of its hands broken off on the threshold” (5:4). The sentence on Eli’s house uses the language of God’s judgment on a pagan god. A priesthood that behaves like a pagan shrine will be judged like one.
reflections.q: “I will cut off your arm” uses an image found nowhere else in the Old Testament, and it is acted out literally three chapters later, when the idol Dagon is found fallen before the ark with “both the palms of its hands broken off on the threshold” (5:4).

reflections.title: The Long Shadow of Unchecked Sin
reflections.html: The fulfillment unfolds over generations. It began at Aphek, where Hophni and Phinehas died (4:11), continued at Nob, where Saul’s man Doeg killed eighty-five priests of Eli’s line in one day (22:18–19), and ended when Solomon removed Abiathar, “that he might fulfill the word of the LORD … concerning the house of Eli” (1 Kings 2:27). This is not guilt passed to innocent people, but a forfeited office and a broken legacy. A father’s passivity can cost his household for generations.
reflections.q: The fulfillment unfolds over generations.

32.brief: Eli will see an enemy in the LORD’s dwelling place even while God does good for Israel, and there will never be an old man in his house. Judgment on Eli’s house does not mean the LORD has abandoned His people.
32.explain:
“And you will see an enemy in My dwelling place,”

Eli “will see an enemy in My dwelling place.” The phrase likely refers to distress or calamity coming upon the sanctuary. Eli would live to hear of the ark's capture by the Philistines (4:17–18).

“despite all the good which God does for Israel.”

The judgment would fall on Eli's house “despite all the good which God does for Israel.” Judgment on Eli's house does not mean the LORD has abandoned His people. God would continue doing good for Israel, even while Eli's family suffered.

“And there shall not be an old man in your house forever.”

God repeats the judgment for emphasis: “there shall not be an old man in your house forever.” The word “forever” echoes the earlier promise that Eli's house would walk before God “forever” (2:30). The promise of permanent privilege had become a sentence of permanent loss.
32.notes:
The Hebrew of the first clause is difficult. It may be read ‘you will see distress in My dwelling place’ or ‘you will look on with envy.’

Verses 31–32 are shorter in the Septuagint, which lacks the last clause of verse 31 and the first clause of verse 32. A Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel also lacks the last clause of verse 31. Translations differ.

reflections.title: God Will Not Stay Where He Is Despised
reflections.html: “And you will see an enemy in My dwelling place, despite all the good which God does for Israel.” The word can mean an adversary or simply distress, the affliction of God’s own tabernacle. Eli lived to hear that the ark was taken (4:17–18), and within a few chapters Shiloh ceased to be God’s dwelling: “go now to My place which was in Shiloh … and see what I did to it” (Jeremiah 7:12; Psalm 78:60). His grandson would be named Ichabod, “the glory has departed” (4:21). God’s presence is His gift, not the guaranteed property of a corrupt priesthood. A religious institution can keep its building and its schedule long after the glory has left.
reflections.q: “And you will see an enemy in My dwelling place, despite all the good which God does for Israel.”

reflections.title: Distress Amid Israel’s Good
reflections.html: Meanwhile God would do good for Israel through Samuel (7:3–14). The punishment mirrors the sin: they greedily took the fat of the land in the present, and they would be cut off from the good God poured out on Israel in the future. Blessing can be flowing all around a person while he experiences only the distress his own compromise has invited.
reflections.q: Meanwhile God would do good for Israel through Samuel (7:3–14).

33.brief: Those of Eli’s men who are not cut off from the altar will remain only to consume his eyes and grieve his heart, and all his descendants will die in the flower of their age. The judgment will bring continuing sorrow, not a single blow.
33.explain:
“But any of your men whom I do not cut off from My altar”

Not all of Eli's descendants would be cut off immediately. Some would remain in priestly service.

“shall consume your eyes and grieve your heart.”

But those who remained would be a source of grief. “Consume your eyes” pictures eyes worn out with weeping. Those who survived would bring sorrow rather than comfort.

“And all the descendants of your house shall die in the flower of their age.”

Eli's descendants would “die in the flower of their age,” in the prime of life. The judgment would bring continuing sorrow, not a single blow.
33.notes:
Abiathar, Eli's descendant, escaped the massacre at Nob (22:20) and served David, but Solomon later removed him from the priesthood for supporting Adonijah, “that he might fulfill the word of the LORD which He spoke concerning the house of Eli at Shiloh” (1 Kings 2:27).

The Septuagint and a Dead Sea Scroll read ‘shall die by the sword of men,’ instead of “in the flower of their age.” The Hebrew text followed by the NKJV reads ‘as men,’ understood as in their prime.

reflections.title: Eyes That Would Be Consumed
reflections.html: “But any of your men whom I do not cut off from My altar shall consume your eyes and grieve your heart.” The phrase pictures eyes failing from weeping (Leviticus 26:16; Lamentations 2:11). In Eli’s own story the words became literal: his eyes “began to grow so dim that he could not see” (3:2), and at the end “his eyes were so dim that he could not see” (4:15). The man who would not look squarely at his sons’ sin lived to have his eyes fail at the sanctuary. Refusing to see sin in those we love does not make it disappear; it leaves our eyes to be consumed by its results.
reflections.q: “But any of your men whom I do not cut off from My altar shall consume your eyes and grieve your heart.”

reflections.title: The Anguish of the Survivor
reflections.html: Sometimes sudden death is a mercy compared with the judgment of outliving your legacy and watching everything you built rot from the inside out. Survival for Eli’s line would be a curse of grief rather than a blessing of continuation, its descendants dying in the prime of life, perhaps by the sword (the Greek text reads “by the sword of men”). The one man spared “from My altar” fits Abiathar, spared at Nob (22:20) and later sent home to Anathoth (1 Kings 2:26).
reflections.q: Sometimes sudden death is a mercy compared with the judgment of outliving your legacy and watching everything you built rot from the inside out.

34.brief: The LORD gives Eli a sign: his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will both die in one day. This sign will confirm the certainty of the whole word spoken against his house.
34.explain:
“Now this shall be a sign to you that will come upon your two sons, on Hophni and Phinehas:”

God gives Eli a “sign,” an event that would confirm the truth of the whole prophecy. The sign concerns “your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas.”

“in one day they shall die, both of them.”
