Both sons would die “in one day.” This sign would confirm the certainty of the whole word spoken against Eli's house. When the sign came, Eli would know that the rest of the prophecy would also be fulfilled. The sign was fulfilled in the battle at Ebenezer: “the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died” (4:11).

reflections.title: Two Sons, One Day
reflections.html: “Now this shall be a sign to you that will come upon your two sons, on Hophni and Phinehas: in one day they shall die, both of them.” The sign was given so that Eli would know the rest of the sentence was certain, and it was fulfilled precisely when the ark was captured (4:11). They had sinned together and would die together; bind these tares in a bundle. God graciously gives signs, not only for judgment but to confirm the authenticity of His word, so that when the blow falls it is recognized as His discipline, not tragic coincidence. Eli received the sign years in advance and still did not act. God gives signs not to satisfy curiosity but to awaken, and a warning that is heard but not obeyed becomes a sentence.
reflections.q: “Now this shall be a sign to you that will come upon your two sons, on Hophni and Phinehas: in one day they shall die, both of them.”

reflections.title: His Warnings Are as Sure as His Promises
reflections.html: God’s threats are as true as His promises, and we must not believe only half His word. The God who kept His promise to Hannah kept His warning to Eli. His faithfulness cuts both ways. (The sign reached the next generation too: Phinehas’s widow named her son Ichabod, 4:19–22. Both brothers’ names are probably Egyptian; Phinehas likely means “the Nubian.”)
reflections.q: God’s threats are as true as His promises, and we must not believe only half His word.

35.brief: The LORD promises to raise up for Himself a faithful priest who will act according to what is in His heart and mind, and to build him a sure house that will serve before His anointed king forever. Historically the promise is fulfilled through Zadok’s line (1 Kings 2:27, 35), and in the wider canon it reaches its fullest realization in Christ, the faithful High Priest.
35.explain:
“Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest”

God promises a new priest. “I will raise up for Myself” emphasizes that God will choose and establish him. He will be “a faithful priest,” reliable and trustworthy, in contrast to Eli's sons.

“who shall do according to what is in My heart and in My mind.”

This priest “shall do according to what is in My heart and in My mind.” He would serve according to God's desires and purposes, not his own appetite.

“I will build him a sure house,”

God would “build him a sure house,” an enduring priestly family. “Sure” means firm, established, reliable. Eli's house would fall; the faithful priest's house would stand.

“and he shall walk before My anointed forever.”

The faithful priest would “walk before My anointed forever,” serving before God's anointed king. “My anointed” connects with Hannah's song: “the horn of His anointed” (2:10). Israel still had no king, yet God speaks of the king He would anoint.

Historically, the promise is fulfilled through Zadok's line. When Solomon removed Abiathar, the last prominent priest of Eli's house, “the king put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar” (1 Kings 2:35). Zadok's descendants served as priests in the temple for centuries. Samuel's own faithful service also anticipates the promise in contrast to Eli's sons, but Samuel was not the exclusive fulfillment. In the wider canon, the promise finds its fullest realization in Jesus Christ, who is “a merciful and faithful High Priest” (Hebrews 2:17) and whose priesthood continues forever (Hebrews 7:24–25).
35.notes:
“Sure” translates the Hebrew ne'eman, which describes something made firm, reliable, and lasting. The same Hebrew word describes the “enduring house” the LORD will make for David (25:28), and the related verb describes the establishment of David's house and kingdom in 2 Samuel 7:16 (“shall be established”).

Ezekiel later identifies “the sons of Zadok” as the priests who remained faithful (Ezekiel 44:15).

reflections.title: The Faithful Priest
reflections.html: “Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest who shall do according to what is in My heart and in My mind. I will build him a sure house, and he shall walk before My anointed forever.” The prophecy found partial, temporary fulfillment in Samuel, “established as a prophet” (3:20), who replaced Eli as Israel’s leader, and in Zadok, who replaced Eli’s descendant Abiathar under Solomon (1 Kings 2:27, 35). But its ultimate trajectory is Jesus Christ. Unlike the Levitical priests who served by outward regulation and often failed, Jesus ministers entirely from the inner life, doing exactly what is in the Father’s heart and mind (John 8:29). He is the “merciful and faithful High Priest” (Hebrews 2:17), “faithful to Him who appointed Him” (Hebrews 3:2), whose house is eternal, and who works in perfect union with God forever. Here the container is opened: the hope sealed in this promise is Christ. We find our eternal security not in our own faithfulness but in the faithfulness of the Priest God raised up for Himself. His priesthood is our sure house.
reflections.q: “Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest who shall do according to what is in My heart and in My mind.

reflections.title: Faithful Priest, Sure House: One Word Twice
reflections.html: “Faithful” and “sure” translate the same Hebrew word, ne’eman, “established, reliable.” It returns at key points: “Samuel had been established (ne’eman) as a prophet” (3:20); Abigail tells David the LORD will make him “an enduring (ne’eman) house” (25:28); God promises David, “your house … shall be established (ne’eman) forever” (2 Samuel 7:16), so that “sure house” is the very language of the Davidic covenant. God says of Moses, “He is faithful (ne’eman) in all My house” (Numbers 12:7), which Hebrews applies to Christ, “faithful … as a Son over His own house, whose house we are” (Hebrews 3:2–6). God builds sure houses for faithful servants, and the house He builds outlasts any house we inherit.
reflections.q: “Faithful” and “sure” translate the same Hebrew word, ne’eman, “established, reliable.”

reflections.title: According to What Is in My Heart
reflections.html: “Who shall do according to what is in My heart and in My mind.” “Mind” here is nephesh, “soul.” In verse 16 the priest’s servant was offered “as much as your heart (nephesh) desires”; the old priesthood served its own appetite. The faithful priest will serve God’s desire. The same measure is used of the king: “The LORD has sought for Himself a man after His own heart” (13:14). Faithfulness is measured by whose desire governs the servant: his own appetite, or God’s heart.
reflections.q: “Who shall do according to what is in My heart and in My mind.”

36.brief: Everyone left in Eli’s house will come and bow before this priest for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread, pleading for any priestly position just to eat. The house that seized the best of the offerings will be reduced to begging for bread.
36.explain:
“And it shall come to pass that everyone who is left in your house”

The prophecy ends with the fate of Eli's surviving descendants.

“will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread,”

They would “bow down” to the faithful priest, begging for “a piece of silver and a morsel of bread.” The family that seized the best of the offerings would be reduced to begging for scraps.

“and say, ‘Please, put me in one of the priestly positions, that I may eat a piece of bread.’”

They would plead for “one of the priestly positions,” any lowly office, simply “that I may eat a piece of bread.” The house that had grabbed meat with a three-pronged fork would ask for a crust of bread. The reversal of Hannah's song applies to Eli's house: “Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread” (2:5).
36.notes: The language of the judgment echoes Hannah's song: the full are humbled (2:5), the proud are brought low (2:3, 7), and those who despise God are lightly esteemed (2:30).

reflections.title: From Fork to Begging Bowl
reflections.html: “Everyone who is left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread.” The family that took meat by force (v. 16) will beg for a crust. The “piece of silver” was the smallest coin, and “a morsel of bread” is a mouthful. They wasted the Lord’s heritage, and now they beg their bread. “Bow down” is the posture of worship, now given to a man for food. Hannah had already sung it: “Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread” (v. 5). The chapter that began with a barren woman lifted up ends with a proud house brought low, the great reversal fulfilled; God’s poetic justice is perfectly symmetrical. What we grab from God’s table, we eventually lose at our own.
reflections.q: “Everyone who is left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread.”

reflections.title: Serving God for Bread
reflections.html: “Please, put me in one of the priestly positions, that I may eat a piece of bread.” Eli’s descendants will ask for priestly work, not to serve God, but to eat. It is the same motive that ruined their fathers, now reduced to begging. When the priesthood is pursued for what it gives rather than for Whom it serves, God’s judgment finally reduces the ministers to beggars. A line meant to feast in the presence of God is reduced to begging for a crust because it traded the sacred for the secular. Paul warns of those who “do not serve our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly” (Romans 16:18). Whoever serves God for bread will end up begging for it. Those who serve Him for Himself find that He is their portion. Are we serving God for Himself, or for the bread His service brings us: approval, position, security?
reflections.q: Are we serving God for Himself, or for the bread His service brings us: approval, position, security?

reflections.title: A Descendant of Eli at the Ruins of Shiloh?
reflections.html: Abiathar was sent to his fields at Anathoth (1 Kings 2:26). Jeremiah was “of the priests who were in Anathoth” (Jeremiah 1:1), and many suggest he descended from Abiathar’s line. If so, a descendant of Eli’s house later preached, “Go now to My place which was in Shiloh” (Jeremiah 7:12). This is possible, not certain, but it would mean God turned the heir of a failed house into the voice that told its story.
reflections.q: Abiathar was sent to his fields at Anathoth (1 Kings 2:26).
